bmc__PMC12717768.pdf.text: Background Kompetitive Allele-Specific PCR (KASP) is a fluorescence-based, high-throughput and cost-effective genotyping technology widely used for detecting single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and insertion-deletions (InDels) across various species. However, few software tools are available for automatically designing KASP primers, especially for InDel variations. Results To address the lack of free and user-friendly automated tools for KASP primer design, we analyzed the sequence characteristics of KASP primers and developed a user-friendly program named EasyKASP on the Excel VBA platform. EasyKASP designs KASP primers for both SNP and InDel variations, with an average processing time of only 0.03 s per primer pair. A total of 80 SNP loci and 6 InDel loci with variations of different lengths were selected to validate the KASP markers designed by EasyKASP, all of which were successfully amplified and genotyped using KASP technology. Conclusions EasyKASP is a simple and rapid tool for KASP primer design, demonstrating broad applicability in KASP genotyping studies. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12859-025-06322-x. Keywords: SNP, InDel, KASP primer design, Excel VBA

Advances in high-throughput genome sequencing technology have enabled the sequencing of a vast number of samples, leading to the identification of abundant whole-genome single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) variations [ 1 ]. As a third-generation molecular marker technology, SNPs are considered ideal tool for genetic studies due to their extensive genomic distribution, genetic stability, ease of standardization and compatibility with high-throughput platforms [ 2 ]. High-throughput sequencing technologies offer significant advantages over traditional SNP detection methods such as Sanger sequencing, CAPS, melting curve analysis, SNaPshot, TaqMan probes, and gene chips [ 3 ]. However, these conventional techniques often fail to meet the growing demand for cost-effective, rapid and large-scale genotyping solutions [ 4 ]. Kompetitive Allele Specific PCR (KASP), developed by LGC Biosearch Technologies, combines PCR amplification with competitive allele-specific primer binding and fluorescence detection to enable accurate and cost-effective genotyping of target SNPs or InDel variations [ 5 ]. Compared to other genotyping technologies, KASP exhibits high analytical stability and accuracy, along with great flexibility in the number of SNPs and samples processed [ 6 , 7 ]. It can also supports high-precision dual-allele genotyping for a limited number of target markers, including SNPs and InDels, across large segregating populations or natural germplasm collections [ 8 ]. KASP is compatible with low-, medium-, and high-throughput genotyping formats and can be integrated with automated platforms, making it suitable for a wide range of research and breeding applications [ 9 ]. KASP has been cited in thousands of peer reviewed scientific publications for hundreds of species, with millions of KASP markers identified [ 10 ]. In agricultural research, KASP has been widely applied for fine mapping of target genes, molecular-assisted breeding, germplasm resource identification, and genetic quality control of crop varieties [ 11 – 15 ]. In medical field, KASP has proven valuable for investigating molecular genetic mechanisms of diseases, mapping disease-associated genes, and screening for drug sensitivity and disease susceptibility loci [ 16 ]. The KASP genotyping reaction simply combines three components: template DNA, KASP assay mix and universal KASP master mix. Unlike conventional PCR primers, the KASP assay mix contains three oligonucleotides: two allele-specific competing forward primers, and one common reverse primer. The allele-specific primers are designed to match the two allelic variants of SNPs or InDels, with their 3’ ends located at the corresponding variant sites. Each specific primer includes 21-bp universal tail sequence at the 5’ ends. The common primer follows the same design principles as regular PCR primers. The KASP Master Mix contains two different fluorescent dyes (e.g., FAM and HEX/VIC) and Taq DNA polymerase in an optimised buffer solution. Each dye is attached to a “reporter” oligonucleotide complementary to one of the tail sequences. The use of universal tail sequences eliminates the need to synthesize fluorescent probes for each variant, significantly reducing reagent cost for KASP detection ( https://www.biosearchtech.com/how-does-kasp-work ). Primer design is critical for the accuracy and efficiency of KASP genotyping. In addition to the general requirements for PCR primers—such as optimal primer length, GC content, Tm value, and avoidance of secondary structures [ 17 ], the common KASP primer should have a higher Tm value than the two specific primers. Furthermore, amplification products should be less than 100 bp to ensure efficient amplification. Since the SNP or InDel site defines the 3′ end of the allele-specific primers, the sequences available for primer design are inherently constrained. Currently, several software tools have been developed for allele-specific PCR (AS-PCR) primer design, such as WASP [ 18 ], PolyMarker [ 19 ], KASPspoon [ 20 ] and FastPCR [ 21 ]. However, some of these programs are no longer updated, and few specifically designed for high-throughput KASP primers designing. Therefore, there is an urgent need for specialized software tailored to KASP primer design. Excel VBA (Visual Basic for Applications) is an object-oriented programming language built into Microsoft Excel, capable of performing tasks ranging from simple formatting to complex data analysis and report generation [ 22 ]. Numerous tools have been developed using the Excel VBA platform, significantly accelerating data management and processing while enhancing workflow productivity [ 23 – 27 ]. In primer design, DNA sequences can be treated as a text string in VBA, allowing parameters such as primer length and GC content to be easily calculated in Excel. The extensive function library of Excel provides robust support for developing customized algorithms for KASP primers. In this study, we developed a simple and user-friendly VBA-based tool named EasyKASP within Microsoft Excel. EasyKASP is freely accessible and facilitates efficient design of KASP primers for both SNP and InDel loci. Moreover, its core functionality can be extended to accommodate diverse primer design requirements, highlighting its versatile and broad applicability in genotyping research.

EasyKASP leverages multiple character functions in Excel to analyze DNA sequences for KASP primer design. The FIND function scans the DNA sequence to locate variation sites and identify repeated bases within primers. Functions such as MID, LEFT, and RIGHT are used to select a strand of DNA sequence as candidate primers, while the LEN function determines primer length. The Do…Loop structure in VBA automates repetitive tasks such as selecting candidate primers, calculating GC content, generating reverse complementary sequences, searching for simple sequence repeat (SSR) and consecutive complementary bases, and evaluating various primer quality parameters. Collectively, Excel’s comprehensive function library provides powerful and flexible platform for designing accurate and efficient KASP primers. The development of EasyKASP is structured into three steps, as illustrated in Fig. 1 . Step 1 Flanking Sequence Analysis. The first step involves identifying the position of the SNP or InDel variation and its flanking sequences in the input sequence, verifying the base at the variation site, and determining the primer design direction based on the GC content and repeated bases within the 25-bp region surrounding the variation site. The strand with a GC content close to 45% and no repeated bases is selected for the specific primer to enhance binding affinity. Step 2 Candidate Primer Selection. The second step focuses on selecting candidate primer sequences and evaluating their parameters. The Tm value, influenced by primer length and GC content, is a crucial parameter for KASP primers. Other factors such as base distribution, repeated bases, complementary bases, and SSR repeat units in the primer are also considered. Step 3 Primer Output. The final step involves organizing and outputting the successfully designed primer sequences. The two specific KASP primers are appended with 21-bp universal tail sequences, while the common primer is reverse complemented. If primers are designed in the reverse direction, the two specific primers are reverse complemented before 21-bp tail sequence addition, and the common primer remains unchanged. Finally, the KASP primers sequence are output to users. The user manual and open-source code are provided in Additional file 1, and the software interface of EasyKASP is provided in file 2, respectively.

EasyKASP requires only four columns of input information to initiate KASP primer design: Loci name, variation type (SNP or InDel), and at least 70 bp of flanking sequence. The target variation site is clearly indicated within square brackets, while other polymorphic sites in the sequence are denoted with ambiguous bases or small brackets. Notably, missing alleles of InDels should not be represented by any value or symbol.

Our previous studies have validated the success rate of EasyKASP in designing primers for SNP loci in cucumber and tomato [ 15 , 28 , 29 ]. To evaluate its application for InDel loci, six InDels with different length of variations in cucumber were selected for KASP primer design [ 30 ]. For SNP genotyping, genomic DNA was extracted from seedlings of 96 hybrid varieties using by SDS method with minor modification [ 31 ]. DNA concentration was measured by Nanodrop 2000 UV Spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA), with final concentrations exceeding 50 ng/µL. The KASP assay mix included two allele-specific primers and one common primer, each diluted to 10 µM and mixed in a ratio of 2:2:5. For each sample, 3 µL of DNA (20–30 ng/µL) and 0.014 µL of KASP assay mix were dispensed into a 384 well plate and dried in oven at 60 °C for 30 min. Then, 3 µL of 1× Master mix (LGC genomics, UK) was added to each well. According to the KASP genotyping manual, PCR was performed with an initial denaturation at 94 °C for 15 min, followed by 10 touchdown cycles (94 °C for 20 s, 61 − 55 °C for 1 min with a 0.6 °C decrease per cycle), and then 26 cycles of 94 °C for 20 s and 55 °C for 1 min (ABI Veriti 384-Well Thermal Cycler). Endpoint fluorescence signals were detected using a PHERAstar (LGC Genomics Ltd, KBS-0021-001) with FAM (λex/em = 485/520 nm) and HEX (λex/em = 535/556 nm) channels. SNP genotypes were determined based on signal clusters: homozygous samples showed one dominant signal while heterozygous samples showed both FAM and HEX signals.

To determine the characteristics and optimal ranges for KASP primers, we analyzed the main parameters of 500 KASP primers successfully used for SNP genotyping in our lab (Additional file 3). Based on this analysis, we empirically established the following formula to calculate the Tm value of KASP primers: Here, LEN is the primer length and GC% is the GC content. This formula was specifically optimized for use with the LGC KASP master mix. The analysis revealed no significant differences in GC content, length, or Tm values between two specific primers. In contrast, the common primer exhibited lower GC content but greater length and higher Tm values than the specific primers (Fig. 2 ). This is attributed to the 21 bp tail sequence added to the 5’end of specific primers. To minimize the total length of specific primers, the strand with higher GC content at the variant site was preferentially selected. EasyKASP, written in VBA, is simple and user-friendly. It requires Microsoft Excel on a PC but does not require an internet connection. After opening the xlsm file containing the program code, users must enable macros and prepare sequences in the format shown in Fig. 3 A. Clicking the “Start” button initiates the primer design process. EasyKASP consumes minimal memory resources and demonstrates high efficiency, designing primers for 20 variant sites in just 0.57 s, with an average of 0.03 s per locus. The results include FAM and HEX primer sequences (specific primers with 21-bp tail sequences, marked in blue and red, respectively) and the common primer sequence (Fig. 3 B). A “Failure” result indicates that no suitable sequence could be designed as KASP primer.

bmc__PMC12717768.pdf.h2: Genotyping of InDel loci using KASP technology
bmc__PMC12717768.pdf.text: EasyKASP has been used to design KASP primers for whole-genome SNP loci in 16 vegetables species [ 1 ], and 80 KASP primers were validated for variety identification in cucumber and tomato [ 15 , 29 ]. To further verify its efficiency for InDel loci, six InDels in cucumber with variation lengths ranging from 1 bp to 50 bp were selected for KASP marker development (Additional file 4). Four InDels were located in functional genes: a 1-bp insertion in CsAPRR2 as controlling the white immature fruit [ 32 ], a 3-bp deletion in CsMLO1 associated with powdery mildew resistance [ 33 ], a 4-bp insertion in CsACS11 involved in sex determination [ 34 ], and 5-bp insertion in CsBADH responsible for fruit fragrance [ 35 ]. The other two InDels, a 34-bp insertion in chromosome 7 and a 50-bp deletion in chromosome 6, were identified in our lab for hybrid variety identification. KASP primers were successfully designed for all six InDels using EasyKASP, and genotypes were accurately determined using KASP technology (Fig. 4 ), demonstrating the tool’s applicability for both SNP and InDel loci.

bmc__PMC12717768.pdf.h2: Wide application of EasyKASP in KASP genotyping
bmc__PMC12717768.pdf.text: With continuous advances in gene function research, phenotype prediction and selection based on genotype has become feasible [ 36 ]. Numerous SNP and InDel variations have been identified from whole-genome resequencing data. SNPs are widely used and actively developed as molecular markers in genetic studies [ 37 ]. Among SNP genotyping methods, KASP offers flexibility, high accuracy, cost-effectiveness, and efficiency [ 38 ]. Primer design software such as Primer3 and Oligo have simplified primer design [ 39 ], but few tools are available for high-throughput KASP primer design. VBA, embedded in Excel, provides powerful functions and loop structures for character recognition and statistical analysis, meeting the requirements for KASP primer design [ 40 ]. In this study, we developed EasyKASP, a VBA-based Excel program for designing KASP primers. A key criterion for primer design software is user-friendly interface that minimizes user effort [ 41 , 42 ]. EasyKASP is easy to install and use, running on any computer with Excel software without requiring an internet connection or parameter selection. Being based in Excel VBA lowers the barrier to entry for many biologists who may not be comfortable with command-line or web-based tools that require specific dependencies. With a single click, users can perform batch and automated KASP primer design. EasyKASP efficiently designs KASP primers in 0.03 s per pair and supports InDel variations. Users can also customize primer design direction and amplicon length by adding invalid bases or deleting raw bases in the sequence.

bmc__PMC12717768.pdf.h2: Comparison of EasyKASP with existing tools
bmc__PMC12717768.pdf.text: We compared EasyKASP with other software tools for KASP primer design (Table 2 ). The main differences lie in efficiency and the ability to design primers for InDels. Kraken, a commercial software developed by LGC Limited, is not free. WASP ( https://bioinfo.biotec.or.th/WASP ) is a web-based software for AS-PCR primer design [ 18 ], while deliberate mismatches can enhance specificity in some contexts, they may reduce PCR efficiency in KASP assays under certain conditions. PolyMarker ( http://www.polymarker.info ) generates SNP markers for hexaploid wheat using local alignments and standard primer design tools to test primers viability [ 19 ]. KASPspoon is an in silico PCR analysis tool for high-throughput SNP genotyping [ 20 ], but both tools only search for primers on one side of the polymorphic site and do not add tail sequence. EasyKASP analyzes the flanking sequences of target variation to determine the optimal direction and candidate region for primers design. If the initial design is unsuccessful, it automatically attempts a design in the opposite direction. This process ensures the user is provided with an optimal KASP primer sequence. FastPCR ( http://primerdigital.com/tools/ ) is a Java-based tool for designing allele-specific PCR primers [ 21 ], but it provides numerous similar primer sequences, making it difficult to select optimal primers. Overall, EasyKASP is free, supports high-throughput design, requires no local installation and automatically adds tail sequences for both SNP and InDel loci.

Not all genetic variations are suitable for KASP assays, and not all KASP primers successfully yield genotyping results. PCR primers must be single-copy in the genome to avoid nonspecific amplification [ 43 ]. Since KASP genotyping relies on fluorescence signals rather than product length, the sequences available for KASP primer design are highly limited. Allele-specific primers can only be selected from 20 to 30 bp upstream or downstream of the SNP/InDel site, and amplicon lengths typically range from 50 to 100 bp. Flanking sequence alignment or primer validation is necessary to ensure PCR product uniqueness. Additionally, non-target variations in flanking sequences must be considered. The quality of the reference genome and sequencing errors may also affect sequence authenticity. Undiscovered variations may exist in immediate proximity to target SNP or InDel loci, which may influence the result of KASP genotyping. For critical genetic variations, Sanger sequencing of the variant and its flanking region is recommended before designing KASP primers.

KASP is a high-throughput, fluorescence-based genotyping technology, yet accessible tools for designing KASP primers remain limited. To address this gap, we developed EasyKASP, a free and user-friendly tool on the Excel VBA platform that enables high-throughput design of KASP primers for both SNP and InDel variations. This implementation demonstrates the robust capability of Excel VBA for molecular assay design, with promising potential for adaptation to other PCR-based primer development applications.

bmc__PMC12729160.pdf.text: The rapid development of single-cell sequencing technologies has provided a robust technical support for the efficient resolution of multiple levels of molecular information from a single-cell population. However, the data produced by these technologies often contain a lot of noise and differences in characteristics that make it difficult to integrate and analyze single-cell multi-omics data. In this study, there is a growing demand for methods to integrate single-cell multi-omics data, which is expected to enhance the ability to reveal cellular heterogeneity and provide new biological perspectives for a deeper understanding of cellular phenotypes by jointly analyzing multi-omics data. We propose LONMF, a non-negative matrix factorization algorithm combining graph Laplacian and optimal transmission to enhance clustering performance and interpretability. We apply LONMF to visualize and cluster multi-pair single-cell multi-omics data, including 10X-multi-group, CITE-seq, and TEA-multi-group seq, to facilitate marker characterization and gene ontology enrichment analysis and to provide rich biological insights for downstream analyses. Our comprehensive benchmarking demonstrates that LONMF exhibits comparable performance compared with the current state-of-the-art in cell clustering and outperforms other methods in terms of biological interpretability. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12859-025-06301-2. Keywords: Single-cell multi-omics, Paired data, Non-negative matrix decomposition, Data integration, Optimal transmission, Graph laplacian

With the rapid development of single-cell multi-omics technologies, we can simultaneously capture and integrate multiple molecular features of the genome, transcriptome, and proteome at the single-cell level [ 1 – 4 ]. These technologies have significantly improved our ability to resolve cellular states while deepening our understanding of the complexity of biological systems [ 5 – 9 ]. In particular, acquiring paired multi-omics data with multiple molecular signatures from the same cell opens up new possibilities for integrative analyses. These paired multi-omics data have helped us to reveal the dynamics of cellular functions and states and have facilitated in-depth exploration of cellular heterogeneity, gene regulation, and developmental mechanisms [ 10 – 13 ]. Due to the high dimensionality and complexity of single-cell multi-omics data, there is an urgent need to develop analytical methods capable of integrating these paired data to accurately capture the synergistic relationships between molecular levels. Based on this, integration methods developed in recent years can accurately capture associations between multi-omics levels, such as regulatory networks of gene expression or protein functions concerning genomic changes [ 14 , 15 ], while significantly improving the accuracy of analyses and reducing the noise and bias of traditional methods. To this end, many advanced methods for integrating unpaired and paired single-cell multi-omics data have been developed [ 16 – 21 ]. For unpaired single-cell multi-omics data integration methods, such as LIGER [ 16 ], integral non-negative matrix factorization (iNMF) is employed to integrate data. Due to the non-convex nature of the problem, results may be sensitive to initialization. This method identifies shared cell types across individuals, species, and modalities (e.g., gene expression, epigenetics, spatial transcriptomics) while capturing dataset-specific features, enabling unified analysis of heterogeneous single-cell data. GLUE [ 17 ] is a modular integration framework that handles unpaired single-cell multi-omics data and infers cross-omics regulatory relationships. By explicitly modeling regulatory networks, GLUE establishes biologically intuitive connections across different omics feature spaces. eMCI [ 18 ] is an interpretable deep neural network-based multimodal integration model that fuses scRNA-seq and spatial transcriptomics data. It excels in cell type classification and deconvolution tasks, identifying key spatial features through attribution analysis and revealing cell type-specific and cell communication spatiotemporal patterns. For paired single-cell multi-omics data integration methods, such as MOFA + [ 19 ], which reconstructs a low-dimensional data representation using multi-omics factor analysis and efficient variational inference, while supporting flexible sparsity constraints for joint modeling across multiple sample groups and modalities. Cobolt [ 20 ] is a multimodal variational autoencoder (MVAE) based approach to generate modality-independent unified representations for the combined analysis of paired multi-omics data. Furthermore, Mowgli [ 21 ] is an approach that effectively integrates paired multi-omics data by combining non-negative matrix decomposition with optimal transmission strategies, thereby enhancing the clustering performance and interpretability of the results. These innovative approaches for paired multi-omics data can more efficiently mine inter-cell shared and complementary information than traditional unpaired data integration methods, thereby greatly advancing the theoretical and practical progress of single-cell multi-omics data integration. Non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) [ 22 ] is commonly used in single-cell multi-omics data integration to reduce high-dimensional data into a low-dimensional space, enabling the extraction of biologically interpretable features. Various extended NMF models have also been developed. For example, JNMF [ 23 ] projects heterogeneous data into a unified coordinate system, facilitating the construction of multidimensional modules; sNMF [ 24 ] incorporates semi-orthogonal constraints to enhance data representation and improve the interpretability of clustering results; and JSNMF [ 25 ] integrates transcriptomic and epigenomic data, using consensus map fusion to address the discrepancy between feature scales and noise levels. However, classical NMF is inherently limited by its linearity assumptions, which limits its ability to model complex nonlinear relationships and higher-order interactions in multi-omics data. The Laplace matrix is essential for the integration and analysis of single-cell multi-omics data. By constructing inter-cell graph structures, it captures similarities between samples, thereby revealing the data’s local geometric features and global topological relationships. Taking paired multi-omics analysis as an example, this method not only identifies shared features among cells but also preserves the modality specificity of the data. Particularly suited for high-dimensional, high-noise datasets, it constructs low-dimensional embeddings that reflect cellular heterogeneity, significantly enhancing the accuracy and biological interpretability of integrated analyses. In this paper, we present a new non-negative matrix factorization algorithm, LONMF, based on graph Laplacian and optimal transmission. This algorithm is designed for integrative analysis of paired single-cell multi-omics data. The method not only more efficiently captures the similarity between single-cell histological modalities to construct complex relationships between modalities but also reveals the high-dimensional geometric structure of each histology in the original data. The superior clustering performance of the method, as demonstrated by its effectiveness in analyzing datasets such as PBMC 10X, the Liu dataset, and CITE-seq, indicates its superiority over other state-of-the-art methods. The examination of the three modal datasets by LONMF not only accurately distinguishes the inter-specificity of immune cells but also yields profound biological insights into the classification of immune cell subpopulations.

The data preparation stage of this study is conducted using the Python packages Scanpy [ 26 ] and Muon [ 27 ]. The LONMF preparation of single-cell RNA sequencing gene expression profiles proceeds as follows: initially, quality control, gene filtering, and cell filtering based on bespoke criteria are performed. Subsequently, the gene expression matrix is normalized and log-transformed, and the genes exhibiting the greatest variability are identified. The preparation of scATAC-seq expression profiles mirrors that of scRNA-seq, with the the following steps: initially, quality control of cells and peak and cell filtering are conducted according to bespoke criteria. Subsequently, the peak expression matrix is normalized and log-transformed, and peaks exhibiting high variability are identified. The preparation of scADT-seq expression profiles involves solely normalizing the data without implementing quality control, protein, or cell filtering. Due to the biological and technical nature of the datasets, the first 1500 highly variable genes and 1500 peaks are selected for the Liu dataset, the first 2500 highly variable genes and 5000 peaks are selected for the PBMC 10X(RNA + ATAC) dataset, and for the TEA dataset, 2500 highly variable genes and 15,000 peaks are selected. Similarly, for the OPCITE and PBMC 10X(RNA + ADT) datasets, the first 2500 highly variable genes and 15,000 peaks are assigned.

To achieve this, Laplacian plots are employed to capture the high-dimensional geometric structure of each data set. The Laplacian matrix plays a crucial role in integrating and analyzing single-cell multi-omics data. Its construction process involves treating cells as nodes in a graph and establishing weighted edges based on molecular feature similarity, thereby generating an adjacency matrix and computing the Laplacian matrix. With its unique spectral properties, it can simultaneously characterize both the local geometric structure and global topological relationships of the data, demonstrating outstanding performance in tasks such as dimensionality reduction, clustering, and feature selection. In multi-omics integration, the Laplacian matrix captures common structural patterns across different modalities while preserving their distinct characteristics, thereby providing robust support for unified modeling of complex heterogeneous data.

bmc__PMC12729160.pdf.h2: LONMF provides superior clustering performance for datasets while enhancing data visualization
bmc__PMC12729160.pdf.text: We benchmark LONMF, MOFA + , Integrated NMF, Cobolt, and Mowgli based on their embedding and clustering performance on these two single-cell multi-omics datasets (RNA + ADT) (Fig. 2 a, c). We selected these two datasets across different sequencing technologies, tissues, and sizes: (i) PBMC 10X (RNA + ADT) is a 10X multi-omics human PBMC dataset from 10X Genomics; (ii) OP CITE is a human bone marrow dataset from Open Problems [ 30 ] CITE-seq. Supplementary Table S1 lists the patterns, number of cells, and cell types for each dataset used in this paper. For more information on data preprocessing, see Methods. Meanwhile, as shown in Fig. 2 a, b, LONMF can process large single-cell multi-omics datasets and provide embedding and clustering performance with state-of-the-art clustering to investigate the profiles of protein modifications and gene expression in human cells. Based on silhouette scores, LONMF outperforms other methods in PBMC 10X (RNA + ADT) and OP CITE. Regarding ARI across resolutions, LONMF outperforms almost all other methods in the OP CITE; Integrated NMF performs best overall on the PBMC 10X dataset. Regarding purity scores, LONMF outperforms the different methods on the OP CITE and PBMC 10X datasets. Overall, LONMF achieves the highest silhouette scores and purity scores with good clustering performance (Fig. 2 a, b). The UMAP plot in Fig. 2 c gives a qualitative intuition of the performance of each method. In OP CITE, only integrated NMF, Cobolt, Mowgli, and LONMF correctly separate subpopulations of B cells. In PBMC 10X (RNA + ADT), LONMF and Mowgli separated better than the other methods.

bmc__PMC12729160.pdf.h2: LONMF enables robust visualization and deep biological insights into cell subpopulations
bmc__PMC12729160.pdf.text: On the PBMC 10X dataset (RNA + ATAC), we compare the clustering performance of LONMF with MOFA + , integrated NMF, Cobolt, and Mowgli. Based on silhouette scores, LONMF outperforms the other methods on this dataset. In terms of Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) across resolutions, LONMF performs best, while in terms of purity scores, MOFA + shows a slight advantage over LONMF, and both are superior to other comparative methods. Overall, LONMF achieves the highest silhouette scores and a high purity score with good clustering performance. (Fig. 3 a). In addition, the UMAP plot in Fig. 3 b provides a qualitative comparison of the methods on the PBMC 10X (RNA + ATAC) dataset. As can be seen from the plots, the LONMF and Mowgli methods cluster cells of the same cell type more tightly, outperforming the other methods. In further analysis, we construct a heatmap of factors versus cell types (see Supplementary Fig. S4 of Supplementary Materials 1), which clearly illustrates the specific expression patterns of each factor across different cells. Based on this, we focus particularly on Factor 8 and Factor 10. Violin plots show that CD56 bright NK cells have higher values in factor 8, while memory B cells have higher values in factor 10 (Fig. 3 c). Based on the gene scores defined by scAI [ 31 ], we plot the gene rankings (Fig. 3 d). Specifically, for factor 8, we divide the expression value of each gene by the sum of the expression values of all genes in the factor, highlighting the 10 marker genes for CD56 bright NK cells in CellMarker 2.0 [ 32 ] (KLRF1, TRDC, NCAM1, SPON2, NCR1, FGFBP2, TBX21, CCL4, CD160, CD38) that scored high in factor 8. Similarly, for factor 10, we use the same calculation method to highlight 10 marker genes for memory B cells (ATM2, CD79A, FCRLA, MS4A1, TNFRSF13C, BANK1, CD79B, VPREB3, IGHF1, PAX-5), and the gene scores for these marker genes are also generally higher in factor 10. For factor 8, we rank genes based on expression levels and select the top 100 genes as specific genes. We then perform GO biological process (BP) enrichment analysis using the ClusterProfiler R package. The analysis employs the Benjamini–Hochberg method to adjust the corrected p -values from Fisher’s exact test, with results expressed as log-10 corrected p -values. The screening threshold is set at 0.001, identifying 96 significantly enriched biological processes (Supplementary Materials 2, Table 1 ). Results indicate that Factor 8 is significantly enriched in biological processes related to leukocyte-mediated immunity and cell surface receptor signaling involved in regulating the immune response. This finding aligns with the characteristics of the CD56-high natural killer (NK) cell subset. CD56-high NK cells regulate the functions of other immune cells by secreting immune factors such as IFN-γ and TNF-α [ 33 ]. Their cell surface receptors are regulated through signaling pathways, including PI3K-AKT and JAK-STAT, which play crucial roles in chronic inflammation, viral infections, and tumor immunity [ 34 ]. Consequently, they have become a key focus in immunotherapy research. For Factor 10, 48 significant biological processes are screened using the same method (Supplementary Materials3, Table 2 ). Results indicate that Factor 10 is significantly enriched in biological processes related to leukocyte-mediated immunity and cell surface receptor signaling involved in immune response regulation. Memory B cells constitute a crucial B cell subset within the adaptive immune system, primarily functioning to rapidly recognize and respond to previously encountered antigens. During secondary immune responses, memory B cells recognize antigens via high-affinity B-cell receptors (BCRs) and rapidly differentiate into antibody-secreting cells. Their function is closely linked to antigen receptor signaling pathways and BCR signaling pathways. BCR-mediated signaling activates downstream molecules (such as SYK and BTK), promoting cell proliferation, antibody secretion, and immune responses [ 35 ]. The BCRs of memory B cells possess higher affinity than those of naive B cells, enabling faster and more efficient responses during secondary immune responses. In addition, we use the GREAT tool ( http://great.stanford.edu/public/html/)to perform an online GO BP enrichment analysis of the top 1000 ranked loci in each factor. The filtering criteria are Binom raw P -value < 0.001 and Binom FDR Q-value < 0.001. The analysis shows that Factor 8 and Factor 10 are significantly enriched in several immune system-related biological processes, including immune response (Factor 8: ; Factor 10: ), regulation of immune system process (Factor 8: ; Factor 10: ) and positive regulation of immune system process (Factor 8: ; Factor 10: ). These enrichment results suggest that factor 8 and factor 10 may play critical functions in specific cell types, providing important functional insights for further studies.

bmc__PMC12729160.pdf.h2: In a variety of data environments, LONMF performs well in cell embedding and clustering tasks
bmc__PMC12729160.pdf.text: We apply LONMF to the Liu dataset to evaluate its embedding and clustering performance, while several data transformations are performed for different distribution scenarios of the three groups of cells. To more realistically simulate the distribution scenarios of the three groups of cells, we apply different transformations to a simple dataset consisting of scCAT-seq. The scCAT-seq dataset provides a combined analysis of scRNA and scATAC for the HCT116, HeLa-S3, and K562 cell lines. Unlike simulated data, this approach avoids making assumptions about the data distribution. Generating simulated data according to a Gaussian distribution, for example, will tend to favor methods that approximate single-cell data with a similar distribution. We design three scenarios to model realistic challenges in multi-omics integration: (i) RNA mixing and mixing of the two scenarios, including two types of cell populations, one of which is mixed in scRNA but completely segregated in scATAC, and the other of which is mixed in scRNA but well segregated in scATAC, or mixed in scATAC but well segregated in scRNA; (ii) rare cell populations, i.e., cell populations that are significantly less numerous than other cell populations; (iii) 82\% sparse, 90\% sparse, and 96\% sparse. Scenario (i) is used to assess the ability of different methods to handle the complementarity of multi-omics data; scenario (ii) is used to test the effectiveness of the methods in recovering rare cell populations; and scenario (iii) is used to test the robustness of the methods to cope with dropout noise while preserving the true pattern of loss in single-cell data. Specific details on dataset generation can be found in the Methods section. We then benchmarked LONMF, Mowgli, MOFA + , NMF, and Cobolt (Fig. 4 a, b, e). We also compare the effectiveness of different methods for UMAP visualization on the Liu dataset (Fig. 4 c, d, f).

bmc__PMC12729160.pdf.h2: LONMF enhances biological interpretability and identifies key immune cell subpopulations in TEA-seq data through cell-type-specific factors
bmc__PMC12729160.pdf.text: We benchmark LONMF on the TEA-seq dataset of human PBMCs to evaluate its biointerpretability. The TEA-seq dataset is a single-cell, multi-omics dataset that contains information on gene expression, chromatin accessibility, and tagged proteins and provides an opportunity for method testing to fully account for the complementarity of molecular regulatory hierarchies. We independently apply MOFA + , Mowgli, and LONMF to the three histological integration analyses of the TEA-seq data and cluster the embedded results generated by each of the three methods. Since cellular annotations are not provided in the dataset, we annotate the clustered results with cell types in combination with gene and protein markers (Fig. 5 a, b). This process successfully identifies major immune cell types, including CD4T cells, CD8T cells, B cells, natural killer (NK) cells, MAIT T cells, monocytes, and erythroid cells. Notably, the consistency of the cell type annotation results of MOFA + , Mowgli, and LONMF is as high as 98%, which is in high agreement with that of Azimuth’s RNA-based annotation results (see Fig. 5 c), suggesting that each of these methods can accurately recover the expected cell types by clustering their embedded data. In addition, we quantify the performance of the LONMF factors using a specificity score based on the Mowgli definition, and the results are shown in bold in Fig. 5 d. The analysis shows that LONMF performs well in establishing one-to-one associations between the factors and cell types, and the specificity scores stood out significantly, especially in NK cells, CD8T cells, and CD4T cells. The high selectivity of the LONMF factors efficiently captures the specific biological features of these cell types. Meanwhile, the specificity analysis of LONMF factors is robust to hyperparameter selection (see Supplementary Fig. S5 of Supplementary Materials 1), further validating its reliability in biological interpretability. Finally, we focus on the biological relevance of the factors identified by LONMF in Human PBMC TEA-seq data. Based on Mowgli [ 21 ], LONMF is able to identify multiple factors associated with subpopulations of cell types, e.g., distinguishing between memory B cells and naive B cells, while capturing specific features of different subpopulations of CD8 T cells, monocytes, dendritic cells, and NK cells. The association of these factors with specific immune subpopulations is determined based on top genes and proteins in effector memory CD8 T cells, naive B cells, memory B cells, and CD56dim NK cells. For other cell populations, we determine associations by analyzing correlations between factor weights and weights of known protein markers. Specifically, we quantify LONMF factors associated with specific immune subpopulations in the TEA-seq PBMC dataset, including CD56 bright NK cells, naive CD4 T cells, plasmacytoid dendritic cells, and conventional dendritic cells. By comprehensively evaluating the ranking of top protein markers among factors, Pearson correlations between factors and protein markers, and scatter plots, we provide insight into the associations between these factors and immune subpopulation characteristics. The LONMF factor 13 is predominantly driven by CD56, with a low contribution from CD16, and its high weight coincide with low CD16 and high CD56 characteristics [ 34 ], fully reflecting the biology of CD56 bright NK cells (Fig. 6 a). Among the 50 factors, factor 13 is the only one with a high Pearson correlation with CD56 and a low correlation with CD16, while CD56 ranks first among the top genes of factor 13 (see Supplementary Figs. S6 , S7 , S8 of Supplementary Materials 1). Conventional dendritic cells (cDC) are characterized by high expression of FceRI [ 36 ]. LONMF factor 44 is driven by FceRI, and its high weight is highly consistent with high FceRI expression, and it is the only factor with a high Pearson’s correlation with FceRI (Fig. 6 a). Plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDC) are phenotypically characterized as CD304-positive and CD14-negative [ 37 ]. LONMF factor 35, which is primarily driven by CD304 and contributes less to CD14, is highly consistent in its high weighting with high CD304, demonstrating a strong correlation with pDC biological characteristics (Fig. 6 a). Naive CD4 T cells are characterized by high CD4 expression and higher levels of CD45RA than CD45RO [ 38 ]. LONMF factor 34 is driven by CD4, and its high weight reflect the expression characteristics of high CD4, high CD45RA, and low CD45RO simultaneously, which is highly consistent with the biological characteristics of naive CD4 T cells (Fig. 6 a). Figure 6 b shows a UMAP plot of LONMF, which visualizes the similarity between factor weight distributions and their associated immune subpopulation protein marker activities. Supplementary Fig. 6 shows UMAP visualization results for all factors and marker proteins. LONMF identifies key genes, proteins, and transcription factors in several immune cell subpopulations. For example, in CD56dim NK cells (factor 12), genes such as NCAM1 (CD56), KLRF1, and GZMB, which are associated with NK cell function, and EOMES, TBX21, and MAFF, which regulate differentiation and effector functions, were detected [ 39 ]. For native B cells (factor 43), LONMF recognizes genes such as FCER2 (CD23), classical B cell markers such as CD19 and CD21, as well as EBF3 and NF-B (REL/RELA), which are closely related to development and function [ 40 ]. For memory B cells (factor 44), top genes include IGHA1 and IGKC, top proteins include CD19 and HLA-DR, and transcription factors associated with their differentiation and homing include RELA, TCF4, and MAX::MYC [ 41 ]. Finally, in effector memory CD8 T cells (Factor 39), LONMF extracts CRTAM associated with cytotoxicity, the memory T cell marker CD45RO, and the key transcription factor EOMES [ 42 ]. These results demonstrate that LONMF is able to accurately capture the biological characteristics of different immune subpopulations.

Currently, several technologies have enabled multi-omics analysis of the same set of cells, and with the rapid development of single-cell multi-omics sequencing technologies, the volume of multi-omics data from a single cell continues to increase, further emphasizing the need and urgency to develop data integration methods. Here, we propose LONMF, a non-negative matrix factorization algorithm based on graph Laplacian and optimal transfer, to integrate different sets of cell data. We thoroughly evaluate the performance of LONMF in cell embedding and clustering tasks by selecting the PBMC 10 × dataset, the CITE-seq dataset, and the scCAT-seq dataset of cancer cell lines for testing, and performing a comprehensive comparative analysis using metrics such as ARI, silhouette coefficient, and purity coefficient. The results show that LONMF outperforms the other four methods (Mowgli, Cobolt, MOFA +, and NMF) in terms of overall performance. This further demonstrates that LONMF is able to effectively preserve the high-dimensional structure of multi-omics datasets while providing significant advantages in the integrated analysis of multi-omics data. In addition, LONMF demonstrates excellent potential in controlled experiments on cancer cell line scCAT-seq datasets, even under challenging conditions. Second, LONMF shows good interpretability. In the PBMC 10 × dataset (RNA + ATAC), in-depth analysis of Factor 8 and Factor 10 revealed that these two factors are highly correlated with immune cells CD56 bright NK cells and memory B cells, respectively. Further Gene Ontology (GO) Biological Process (BP) enrichment analysis of these two factors shows that they are highly correlated with leukocyte-mediated immunity and immune response-regulated cell surface receptor signaling. The results show that they are closely related to key biological processes such as “leukocyte-mediated immunity” and “immune response-regulated cell surface receptor signaling”. Additionally, we evaluate LONMF’s performance on TEA-seq data, demonstrating its capability to establish one-to-one correlations between factors and cell types. The method successfully captures the unique biological characteristics of NK cells, CD8 T cells, CD4 T cells, and others. Furthermore, LONMF generates biologically meaningful results when applied to paired single-cell RNA sequencing, single-cell ATAC sequencing, and surface protein analysis data. Combined with the clinical significance of CD56, CD16, FceRI, and CD304, among others, the unique characterization of immune cell subpopulations in the immune response is revealed. In particular, the relationship between CD56 and NK cell function, the role of CD16 in antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxic responses, and the contribution of FceRI and CD304 in allergic reactions and antiviral immunity suggest that the combined analysis of these markers contributes to a more comprehensive understanding of the complexity of the immune system. With this approach, key immune cell subpopulations and biomarkers can be accurately identified, providing strong support for the design of personalized protocols for clinical immunotherapy. Meanwhile, the robustness of the hyperparameter is investigated, and the experimental results show that the clustering performance of LONMF remains stable across different instances, a finding that is validated by varying the parameter values. The computational efficiency of LONMF is shown in Supplementary Table S3 of Supplementary Materials 1. Due to its relatively high computational complexity, its operational efficiency is slightly lower compared to other methods. However, LONMF demonstrates excellence in clustering performance and biological interpretability, thereby retaining significant potential value for practical applications and subsequent analyses. However, all benchmarks focusing on paired multi-omics integration face an important limitation, namely the lack of high-quality cell biology annotations. Although fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) is an effective stand-alone annotation method in some cases, such annotations are still scarce in the available paired multi-omics data. In addition, exploring potential regulatory relationships between different histological features can provide new perspectives and directions for model optimization and in-depth analysis. LONMF can also be extended to integrate larger datasets, potentially enhancing analytical accuracy and broadening its application potential across multiple research fields.

bmc__PMC12729404.pdf.text: Background Multi-drug combinations represent an effective strategy for treating complex diseases. However, due to the vast number of unknown interactions among drugs, accurately predicting drug–drug interactions (DDIs) is essential for preventing adverse drug reactions that may cause serious harm to patients. Therefore, DDI prediction plays a critical role in pharmacology. Results In this paper, we propose a novel DDI prediction model that integrates a self-attention mechanism with a capsule neural network, termed ACaps-DDI. The model effectively combines chemical information from internal drug substructures with biological information from external drug targets and drug-metabolizing enzymes to predict potential drug-drug interactions. Conclusions Experimental results on two benchmark datasets show that the ACaps-DDI model outperforms six other classification models across seven evaluation metrics, demonstrating its strong predictive performance and generalization ability. Ablation studies further confirm the effectiveness of individual components within the ACaps-DDI architecture. Finally, case studies involving three drugs (cannabidiol, torasemide, and cyclophosphamide) validate the model’s ability to predict previously unknown drug interactions. In conclusion, the ACaps-DDI model exhibits high predictive accuracy for known drugs and demonstrates promising predictive capability for unseen drugs, highlighting its practical significance for clinical research on drug interactions. Keywords: Drug-drug interactions, Self-attention mechanism, Capsule neural network

Drug-drug interactions (DDIs) refer to the mutual effects that occur when two or more drugs are administered concurrently. The physiological outcomes of taking multiple medications can be beneficial, harmful, or negligible. Beneficial interactions enhance therapeutic efficacy or improve treatment outcomes compared to monotherapy [ 1 ], whereas harmful interactions are classified as adverse drug events (ADEs) [ 2 , 4 ]. According to China’s National Adverse Drug Reaction Monitoring Annual Report (2014), adverse reaction reports among patients aged 65 years and older accounted for 19.9% of all cases. Clinical data further indicate that the incidence of adverse reactions is approximately 6%-8% for individuals taking fewer than five medications, but increases sharply to around 40% for those taking six medications. Polypharmacy, commonly defined as the concurrent use of five or more drugs, has become increasingly prevalent among the elderly population [ 3 ]. Therefore, understanding DDIs to maximize therapeutic efficacy while minimizing adverse drug reactions has received significant clinical and research attention. Despite their clinical importance, experimental validation of DDIs remains highly challenging due to the extensive cost and time required to test the vast number of possible drug combinations. In recent years, with the advancement of computer-aided drug discovery technologies and the continuous accumulation of biomedical data, machine learning (ML) has emerged as a powerful tool for predicting DDIs. Researchers collect drug information from literature and clinical reports to construct comprehensive databases that facilitate computational prediction. ML has achieved notable success in computer vision and bioinformatics [ 5 , 6 ], and it shows substantial potential in DDI prediction. This computational approach effectively mitigates the limitations of traditional clinical trials (e.g., high cost, complexity, and time consumption) by enabling rapid and efficient prediction of potential drug-drug interactions using accumulated biomedical data. A wide range of computational approaches have been developed for predicting drug-drug interactions (DDIs). Early studies primarily relied on conventional machine learning techniques. Li et al. [ 7 ] employed Bayesian networks that integrated molecular and pharmacological phenotypes to predict DDIs. Chen et al. [ 8 ] proposed the HNAI framework, which constructed DDI networks, calculated drug-drug pair similarities based on four feature types, and used five traditional classifiers—Naive Bayes, decision trees, k-nearest neighbors, logistic regression, and support vector machines—for prediction. Sridhar et al. [ 9 ] further developed a scalable probabilistic model to infer DDIs from drug similarity networks derived from known interactions. To improve representation learning, Zhang et al. [ 10 ] introduced a manifold-regularized matrix factorization method with an ensemble learning strategy that achieved superior predictive performance. Zhu et al. [ 11 ] modeled drug dependencies through a dependency network and proposed an attribute-supervised learning model for adverse DDI (ADDI) prediction. With the increasing availability of heterogeneous drug data, several studies incorporated multiple feature sources and deep learning techniques. Rohani et al. [ 12 ] integrated diverse drug information (including substructures, targets, side effects, pathways, transporters, and indications) and used neural networks to predict unknown DDIs. Deng et al. [ 13 ] introduced DDIMDL, a unified deep neural network framework that combines four types of drug features (chemical substructures, targets, enzymes, and pathways) to learn cross-modal representations of drug pairs and predict DDI-related events. Graph neural network (GNN) approaches have become increasingly prominent for DDI prediction. Feng et al. [ 14 ] applied graph convolutional networks (GCNs) to capture topological relationships within DDI networks and used deep neural networks to predict potential interactions. Wang et al. [ 15 ] proposed the MIRACLE model, which views the DDI network as a multi-view graph and employs a key-aware attention propagation mechanism to capture molecular structural information. Nyamabo et al. [ 16 ] developed SSI-DDI, a deep learning framework that directly operates on raw molecular graphs, decomposing DDI prediction into identifying pairwise substructure interactions. Kang et al. [ 17 ] further enhanced GCN-based methods by introducing a hierarchical layer-by-layer fusion rule to aggregate node embeddings, yielding more accurate link predictions. Recent work has focused on more refined drug representations. Li et al. [ 18 ] proposed a dual-view representation learning network that jointly captures local (intra-drug) and global (inter-drug) structural information. Ma et al. [ 19 ] designed a directed message-passing neural network with a substructure attention mechanism to adaptively extract informative molecular substructures, modeling DDIs as pairwise interactions between unique substructures of each drug. Although numerous machine learning approaches have been applied to drug–drug interaction (DDI) prediction, several critical limitations persist. First, many existing methods rely primarily on the intrinsic structural information of drug molecules as input features, while overlooking the relationships between internal molecular substructures and external binding proteins, as well as the integration of heterogeneous biological data sources. In practice, drug-protein interactions exert an indirect yet significant influence on DDI prediction accuracy. Second, feature redundancy remains a major challenge. Direct concatenation of heterogeneous feature vectors often leads to dimensional inconsistencies and redundant representations, underscoring the need for more efficient and flexible strategies to integrate multimodal drug features. Third, some studies implicitly assume that incorporating a greater variety of features will inevitably enhance predictive performance. However, excessive fusion of heterogeneous information such as knowledge graphs, DDI networks, and biological annotations, can instead introduce noise and redundancy, thereby impairing the model’s ability to capture the most informative drug-related patterns. To address the aforementioned limitations, we propose a novel framework named ACaps-DDI for drug-drug interaction (DDI) prediction. The proposed approach first integrates three types of drug features and constructs similarity matrices for each drug using Gaussian similarity. The resulting drug-pair similarity vectors are then processed by a deep neural network to obtain comprehensive representations of drug pairs. Next, a self-attention mechanism is employed to assign adaptive weights to each representation, thereby enhancing both model performance and interpretability. The refined drug-pair representations are subsequently fed into a capsule neural network to perform binary classification of DDIs. The overall workflow of the proposed model is illustrated in Fig. 1 , where substructure molecular graphs are derived from the DrugBank database [ 20 ]. To evaluate the effectiveness of ACaps-DDI, we compare it with six baseline models: k-nearest neighbor (KNN), logistic regression (LR), naive Bayes (NB), random forest (RF), XGBoost (XGB), and DDIMDL. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves superior predictive performance across seven standard evaluation metrics.

DrugBank [ 20 ] is a comprehensive drug database that provides detailed information on 12,151 drugs, including 3,844 FDA-approved drugs and 5,867 experimental drugs. In this study, two datasets were employed to validate the effectiveness of the proposed model: Dataset 1, constructed by Deng et al. [ 13 ], which contains a smaller number of drugs, and Dataset 2, provided by Lin et al. [ 21 ], which includes a larger set of drugs. The dataset from Deng et al. was derived from DrugBank and includes four types of features: chemical substructures, targets, pathways, and enzymes. Pathways were represented as KEGG IDs, which were mapped to the corresponding drug pathway information using the KEGG database [ 22 ]. Drug targets and enzymes were directly obtained from DrugBank. After preprocessing, the dataset contained 572 drugs, 74,528 DDI pairs, and 65 event types. Since our task focuses on binary classification, we modified this dataset by removing pathway features and converting the 65 event categories into two classes to determine whether an interaction exists between two drugs. The dataset from Lin et al. contains 1,258 drugs and 323,539 paired DDIs, with the drugs associated with 100 event categories. The same preprocessing procedure was applied, converting the 100 event categories into two binary classes. The detailed statistics of both datasets are presented in Table 1 .

We constructed a balanced drug interaction dataset that includes both original positive samples and generated negative samples. Negative samples were created by randomly pairing two different drugs to form candidate drug pairs. First, any pair already identified as a positive sample was excluded. Second, we checked for duplication and applied unordered pair processing to ensure that the same drug pair did not appear in reverse order. Next, we calculated the Jaccard similarity between the molecular substructures of the two drugs. Candidate pairs with a similarity greater than or equal to the threshold value of 0.5 were discarded, while those with similarity below the threshold were retained as negative samples. This step ensures that the negative samples are not overly dissimilar from the positive samples, thereby improving the model’s ability to distinguish subtle structural differences. Duplicate pairs and those exceeding the similarity threshold were removed. The negative sample pool was then replenished iteratively until the number of negative samples matched the number of positive samples, resulting in a balanced dataset suitable for binary classification.

The extraction and representation of drug features are crucial for model construction. Previous studies have shown that incorporating more features does not necessarily lead to better model performance [ 12 ]. Therefore, we selected three representative drug features—substructure, target, and enzyme—to provide complementary chemical and biological information. Each drug is represented as a binary feature vector, where the value of 1 or 0 indicates the presence or absence of the corresponding descriptor. According to PubChem [ 23 ], there are 881 predefined substructures, enabling each drug to be encoded as an 881-dimensional vector representing the presence or absence of specific substructure types. Similarly, there are 1,162 drug-associated targets, allowing drugs to be represented as 1,162-dimensional target feature vectors. In addition, 202 enzymes are associated with drugs, and the enzyme features are encoded as 202-dimensional binary vectors. Using this encoding scheme, each drug is represented by three feature vectors corresponding to its substructure, target, and enzyme characteristics. The extracted feature vectors are high-dimensional and highly sparse, with most elements having a value of 0. To address this issue, we applied similarity-based feature compression to reduce sparsity and capture meaningful relationships between drugs. We compared the performance of three similarity metrics: Jaccard similarity, cosine similarity, and Gaussian similarity, and ultimately selected the Gaussian similarity metric to compute the bit vectors and construct the drug–drug similarity matrix. For Dataset 1, we obtained three 572 × 572 drug–drug similarity matrices. Each feature of a drug is represented as a 572-dimensional vector. Therefore, each drug with three types of features is represented by a 3 × 572-dimensional vector. For Dataset 2, we obtained three 1,258 × 1,258 drug–drug similarity matrices. Each feature of a drug is represented as a 1,258-dimensional vector. Accordingly, each drug with three types of features is represented by a 3 × 1,258-dimensional vector.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) can capture both low-order and high-order features of data through multiple layers of neurons, allowing the model to better learn complex patterns. In addition, DNNs can take full advantage of parallel computing platforms such as GPUs to accelerate the training process and improve computational efficiency. In this study, we employ a deep neural network for drug-pair feature extraction. For Dataset 1, the three features of each drug pair are concatenated into 2 × 572-dimensional vectors, which are then used as input to the DNN. The neurons in the hidden layers are computed according to the following equations: The input vector is transformed linearly, where represents the weight matrix between the current hidden layer and the previous layer, denotes the weighted input of the hidden layer, is the bias term, and is the activation function. Finally, the output layer is passed through the following equations: The vectors are then passed through the output layer. represents the predicted output of the network, and the function is used to transform the output into a probability distribution. We employ the DNN to perform dimensionality transformation, using a normalization layer after each hidden layer of neurons to accelerate the convergence of the neural network. The normalization layer adjusts the input data distribution through learnable scaling and translation parameters. Following normalization, a dropout layer with a rate of 0.4 is applied to randomly deactivate a portion of the neurons during training. This reduces dependencies between neurons, enhances the model’s generalization capability, and helps prevent overfitting. The feature vectors of drug pairs are processed through three hidden layers, reducing the dimensionality from 1,144 to 128. This process yields feature vectors for three pairs of drugs. The same procedure is applied to Dataset 2, with corresponding dimensionality adjustments according to the number of drugs in the dataset.

Self-attention mechanisms [ 27 ], as illustrated in Fig. 2 , enable the adaptive assignment of importance weights to different types of information. They have recently achieved remarkable success in various domains, including bioinformatics. Since the representations of the three features of a drug pair contribute unequally to the final DDI prediction result, we adopt a self-attention mechanism based on previous research to assign appropriate weights to each feature. Capsule neural networks [ 28 ] are designed to capture the hierarchical relationships among features and to generate representations that preserve richer semantic and structural information. Compared with conventional neural networks, capsule architectures combined with a dynamic routing algorithm can reduce the number of parameters while improving the model’s parameter efficiency. In this study, we implement a PrimaryCaps layer to extract diverse feature representations through convolutional operations and to maintain consistent vector lengths using nonlinear compression. Specifically, the PrimaryCaps layer is constructed with nine convolutional units, one input channel, one output channel, a convolutional kernel size of (9, 3), and a stride of 1. After the convolution operation, the dimensionality of each sample is transformed to (3,168, 1). A subsequent reshaping operation converts the output to a dimension of (396, 8), resulting in 396 eight-dimensional vector capsules. Finally, the capsule lengths are normalized to the range (0, 1) through a fully connected layer.

The proposed algorithm consists of three main components: data preprocessing, feature extraction, and a neural network-based prediction module. The pseudo-code of the ACaps-DDI algorithm is presented in Table 2 .

We use six categorical evaluation metrics to assess the robustness and effectiveness of our model from different perspectives. These six metrics are Accuracy (ACC), Precision, Sensitivity, F1 score (F1), Specificity, and Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC). The definitions of these metrics are as follows: where TP represents the number of positive samples correctly predicted as positive, FN represents the number of positive samples incorrectly predicted as negative, TN represents the number of negative samples correctly predicted as negative, and FP represents the number of negative samples incorrectly predicted as positive. To provide a more intuitive understanding, the confusion matrix for the binary classification problem is presented in Table 3 . In addition to the aforementioned metrics, we also evaluate the performance of the model using AUC (area under the ROC curve) and AUPR (area under the precision–recall curve). In general, an AUC value closer to 1 indicates better model performance, while a value closer to 0.5 indicates poorer performance. The AUPR ranges from 0 to 1, with higher values representing better classification performance. For the performance evaluation of ACaps-DDI, we plotted the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves and precision–recall (PR) curves, and calculated the areas under both curves as two comprehensive evaluation indicators.

Different similarity calculation methods affect the performance of the ACaps-DDI algorithm. We examined the impact of three similarity metrics—Jaccard, cosine, and Gaussian—on the model’s performance using Dataset 1. The experimental results are presented in Table 4 . Among the three metrics, the Gaussian similarity achieved the best performance, and it was therefore adopted for Dataset 2 to compute the similarity between drugs. The model was trained using five-fold cross-validation, with the number of iterations per round set to 100. Stratified sampling was employed to ensure a consistent distribution of positive and negative samples across all folds. A learning rate scheduler was used to dynamically adjust the learning rate, starting at 0.001, and automatically reducing it when the validation loss plateaued (factor = 0.5, patience = 3). An early stopping mechanism was applied to terminate training if the validation loss did not improve for 10 consecutive rounds, restoring the best-performing model. Gradient clipping was also used to prevent gradient explosion by constraining the gradient norm within a specified threshold.

In this experiment, to verify the performance of the ACaps-DDI model, we applied five-fold cross-validation on both datasets to enhance the credibility of the results. As shown in Fig. 3 , the average AUC values for Dataset 1 and Dataset 2 reached 0.9792 and 0.9979, respectively. As shown in Fig. 4 , the corresponding average AUPR values reached 0.9798 and 0.9978, respectively. The high AUC and AUPR values demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves superior predictive performance. The low variance observed across folds further indicates the stability and robustness of the model. As presented in Table 5 , the accuracy on Dataset 1 is 0.9269, while the accuracy on Dataset 2 reaches 0.9839, suggesting that the model performs better with larger datasets. The MCC scores for the two datasets are 0.8541 and 0.9674, respectively, further confirming that dataset size influences model performance and results.

We conducted ablation experiments on Dataset 1 to verify the effectiveness of each module in the proposed model. The model without the capsule neural network was denoted as A-DDI, and the model without the self-attention mechanism was denoted as Caps-DDI. The performance results of the different model variants on Dataset 1 are presented in Table 6 . The accuracy of ACaps-DDI exceeds that of Caps-DDI and A-DDI by 0.0026 and 0.0039, respectively. In addition, ACaps-DDI demonstrates superior performance across the other six evaluation metrics. These results confirm the contribution and effectiveness of both the self-attention mechanism and the capsule neural network within the proposed framework.

We compared ACaps-DDI with DDIMDL and several widely used classification methods. Since the original DDIMDL framework was designed for multi-classification problems, we modified its final output layer for binary classification while preserving the original network structure. In addition, we compared several traditional machine learning algorithms, including k-nearest neighbor (KNN), logistic regression (LR), naive Bayes (NB), random forest (RF), and XGBoost (XGB). All of these traditional models were trained using one-hot encoding on each of the three feature sets. All experiments were conducted under identical conditions to ensure fair comparison. The performance metrics—Accuracy (ACC), Precision, Sensitivity, Specificity, F1 score (F1), AUC, and AUPR—for all seven models are summarized in Tables 7 and 8 . The results show that the ACaps-DDI model achieved the best performance across these metrics on both datasets. From Table 7 , the ACC value of ACaps-DDI on Dataset 1 is 0.9269, which is 18.64%, 10.55%, 11.55%, 12.14%, 17.40%, and 2.63% higher than those of KNN, LR, NB, RF, XGB, and DDIMDL, respectively. From Table 8 , the ACC value of ACaps-DDI on Dataset 2 is 0.9839, exceeding KNN, LR, NB, RF, XGB, and DDIMDL by 25.38%, 19.33%, 20.16%, 19.66%, 27.78%, and 3.96%, respectively. Furthermore, the AUC and AUPR values of the ACaps-DDI model reached the highest levels on both datasets, confirming its superior predictive capability and generalization performance. From Tables 7 and 8 , it can be observed that as the dataset size increases, the performance of our model on Dataset 2 surpasses that on Dataset 1, and its advantages over other algorithms become even more pronounced on the larger dataset. In conclusion, ACaps-DDI consistently outperforms all other models across all evaluation metrics on two datasets of different sizes, demonstrating the superior performance and generalization ability of the proposed model.

To further demonstrate the validity of the proposed methodology for predicting new drug–drug interactions (DDIs), we conducted an external prediction study using three drugs: Torasemide, Cannabidiol, and Cyclophosphamide. Torasemide [ 30 ] and Cyclophosphamide are commonly used anticancer drugs, while Cannabidiol was initially employed as a potent diuretic and was later found to help control blood pressure and treat edema caused by heart failure, renal disease, and liver cirrhosis [ 29 ]. Exploring the potential interactions among these three drugs is therefore of significant clinical value. We used Dataset 2, which contains 1,258 drugs and 323,539 DDI pairs, to train the model. The trained model was then used to predict the interactions between each of the three selected drugs and the remaining 1,257 drugs, forming an external validation set. In the validation results, a DrugBank indication in the Evidence column denotes that the predicted drug pair is confirmed in DrugBank, while N/A indicates that no validation information is available. Tables 9 , 10 and 11 present the top 20 predicted interaction scores and their corresponding validation results. Specifically, among the top 20 predicted interactions for Torasemide, 13 were confirmed in DrugBank (Table 9 ). For Cannabidiol, 17 of the top 20 predictions were validated (Table 10 ), and for Cyclophosphamide, 17 of the top 20 predictions were also confirmed (Table 11 ). The primary source of prediction errors arises from structural similarities between certain drugs, such as Tianeptine and other compounds interacting with the three target drugs, which can lead to misjudgments by the ACaps-DDI model and subsequent inaccurate predictions. Nevertheless, for drug pairs not present in the training data, the results demonstrate that the ACaps-DDI model can accurately identify potential interactions. Unconfirmed drug interactions can serve as valuable candidates for further experimental or clinical validation to uncover previously unknown DDIs.

In this paper, we proposed ACaps-DDI, a new model for drug–drug interaction (DDI) prediction based on multi-source information fusion. The model effectively integrates internal molecular structures and external protein-related features through deep neural networks, a self-attention mechanism, and capsule neural networks. ACaps-DDI combines three types of drug features (substructure, target, and enzyme) and adaptively assigns importance to each feature using self-attention. The capsule network further enhances feature representation by capturing spatial and hierarchical relationships, overcoming the limitations of traditional convolutional neural networks. Extensive comparison and ablation experiments demonstrate that ACaps-DDI outperforms existing models and that each component contributes significantly to overall performance. Among the tested similarity measures, the Gaussian similarity achieved the best predictive results. In future work, we plan to incorporate additional drug-related information, such as knowledge graphs and DDI networks, to further improve prediction accuracy and enhance the model’s ability to learn from multiple data modalities.

bmc__PMC12750718.pdf.text: Background DNA data storage offers exceptional density and longevity, but its practicality is hampered by the high cost and low throughput of de novo DNA synthesis. A key cost driver in array-based synthesis is the length of a common supersequence required to encode a batch of DNA strands. Objective This study aims to address this cost bottleneck by investigating the optimal batch partitioning of DNA sequences. Our goal is to minimize the total synthesis cost, which is defined as the sum of the lengths of the shortest common supersequences (SCS) across all batches. Results Given a large pool of balanced binary sequences, which is partitioned into k batches with almost equal size, we define the total cost of to be the sum of lengths of the shortest common supersequence (SCS) of all sequences in each batch. The central problem is to determine the minimum total cost of , denoted by , among all partitions into k batches. Conclusions When is the set of all balanced binary sequences of length 2 n , we use combinatorial methods to obtain for any positive n , and for and large n with C a constant depending on k . Similarly, we get for and large n when is the set of all balanced DNA sequences of length 2 n . Previously, the probabilistic model of this problem was studied by Makarychev et al. (IEEE Trans Inf Theory 68:7454–7470, 2022), where strings are unconstrained or without consecutive identical letters.

DNA based data storage systems are particularly appealing owing to their high information capacity and durability. De novo DNA synthesis is a powerful biotechnology which can generate DNA sequences without pre-existing templates. The storage of digital data in synthetic DNA molecules has also received much attention [ 1 – 7 ], but its practical application of existing DNA synthesis technologies is currently severely limited due to its high cost and low throughput [ 8 ]. For example, the cost of synthesizing DNA oligonucleotides using dozens of building blocks can be up to hundreds to thousands of dollars. Currently, the main methods for producing large quantities of DNA molecules is array-based DNA for synthesis [ 8 ]. Using this technique, DNA synthesizers can create large numbers of DNA strands in parallel, with each strand growing one DNA base at a time. This leads to a problem of finding a common supersequence for a given set of strands as an appropriate representative for the set. In order to solve the problem of a large number of DNA molecules exceeding the load of the synthesizer, we follow the methods in [ 9 ] that the DNA strands pool needs to be spilit into batches, with each batch size corresponding to the maximum load of the synthesizer. In DNA synthesis applications, the cost for a batch is proportional to the length of the common supersequence, and the total cost across all batches is proportional to the sum of the lengths of the common supersequences for all batches [ 9 – 11 ]. The mathematical formulation of this problem is as follows. Let be a set of sequences with equal length, and let be an integer. Partition to k subsets (called batches ), , each of size almost . Denote this partition by . Define the cost function to be the length of the Shortest Common Supersequence of all sequences in . Then the problem is to determine the minimum total cost among all partitions of , that is, . To minimize the cost, one problem is to compute the shortest common supersequence of each batch, which is the well-known SCS problem. The SCS problem is known to be NP-hard and remains NP-hard under strict restrictions to the problem instances [ 11 – 13 ]. It has multiple applications in various areas, mainly concluding scheduling, data compression, query optimization, text-editing and DNA sequences assembly in computational biology [ 14 ]. Actually, one can apply SCS to estimate whether different species have the same ancestor. For example, consider a set of DNA strings from different species, if we simply assume the only mutations during evolutionary process is the lost of the DNA in the embryo, then the embryonic DNA string must be the common supersequence of the given DNA strings.
