scirep__PMC12830661.pdf.text: The impact of Dexmedetomidine (Dex) use on the prognosis of patients with ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) remains a subject worthy of further investigation. This study seeks to evaluate the association between Dex administration and prognosis in critically ill patients with VAP. We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the MIMIC-IV database, including adults (≥ 18 years) with VAP and ICU stays ≥ 24 h. Patients were divided into the DEX group and the non-DEX group based on Dex administration. The primary endpoint was in-hospital mortality, and the secondary endpoint was 90-day survival rate. We used multivariable logistic regression and propensity score matching (PSM) to adjust for baseline imbalances. Kaplan-Meier analysis assessed survival differences. Stratified analyses evaluated temporal trends (2008–2022), dosage (mcg/kg/h), and infusion duration (hours) to further validate the robustness of the results. This research included a total of 1766 VAP patients (DEX: n = 905; non-DEX: n = 861), Dex was associated with reduced in-hospital mortality (unadjusted OR 0.55, 95% CI 0.44–0.69; adjusted OR 0.62, 95% CI 0.47–0.83).The survival curve was calculated based on Kaplan-Meier analysis, which indicated that the DEX group exhibited a relatively longer survival time, and this difference was highly statistically significant ( p < 0.001).It is worth mentioning that the mortality reduction remained robust across all sensitivity analyses, including PSM, temporal stratification, and dose-duration subgroups. Dex is associated with significantly lower in-hospital mortality in VAP patients. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1038/s41598-025-33124-1. Keywords: Dexmedetomidine, VAP patients, MIMIC-IV, ICU, In-hospital mortality Subject terms: Diseases, Medical research, Risk factors

VAP is a nosocomial pneumonia 1 that occurs in individuals receiving mechanical ventilation through the application of endotracheal intubation or tracheostomy 2 . VAP is pneumonia that occurs within 48 h after starting mechanical ventilation or after the interruption of mechanical ventilation 3 , and is marked by a high prevalence, ranging from 9% to 70% in studies. It is also marked by increased mortality, generally ranging from 20 to 71% 4 , 5 . Symptoms of VAP include purulent respiratory secretions, fever, respiratory distress, and radiographic evidence of pulmonary infiltration 6 , VAP is generally defined by “mechanical injury” and “biological injury,” complicating treatment and leading to elevated mortality, prolonged mechanical ventilation times, and elevated health costs 7 . Preventive interventions, empirical antimicrobial treatment, and treatments such as combined irrigation and sputum aspiration comprise the primary treatments. These treatments, however, prove ineffective in alleviating symptoms in the early stages of treatment 6 , prompting the need for the identification of therapeutic targets in order to avoid the onset of VAP. Dexmedetomidine (Dex), a highly selective α2-adrenergic receptor agonist 8 , possesses a range of actions such as sedation, analgesia, anti-sympathetic activity, anti-inflammatory activity, hemodynamic stability, and delirium and agitation suppression after surgery 9 , in addition to organ protection 10 . Because of its safety profile and unique mechanism, it is being increasingly utilized in the clinic. It is now being used for pre-anesthetic medication in pediatric and adult populations, procedural sedation 11 , anesthesia supplementation, perioperative pain control, and surgery-induced delirium prevention 12 . Current guidelines suggest Dex as the preferred sedative in ventilated patients, considering that it is effective in sedation and analgesia with hemodynamic stability 13 . The sedative effect is equivalent to that of midazolam and propofol but with less delirium occurrence 14 , 15 . The clinical and research paradigm for Dex is expanding beyond sedation to encompass its significant multi-organ protective effects. Evidence now robustly demonstrates that Dex provides cytoprotection in critical structures such as the heart, brain, lungs, kidneys, liver, and gastrointestinal tract 16 , 17 . These pleiotropic benefits are largely mediated through a confluence of key cellular mechanisms: antioxidative stress, potent anti-inflammation, anti-apoptosis, and precise autophagy regulation 17 , 18 . Clinical evidence indicates that Dex can reduce the degree of inflammatory mediators in early-stage VAP and enhance lung oxygenation 19 , thereby exerting a protective function in lung function. Mechanisms behind such effects would be through reduced inflammatory factors, inhibition of the TLRs/NF-κb signal pathways, downregulation of MUC5AC expression, and enhancement in oxidative stress status 20 . A systematic review of the current evidence suggests 21 that Dex possesses a strong sedation, analgesic, and anti-inflammatory potential with the possibility of improving clinical outcomes in VAP patients. However, most such studies were limited by the lack of proper clinical endpoint markers and by having small sample populations—factors critical in establishing the efficacy of interventions against VAP. The precise benefits and the mechanisms through which Dex is effective in VAP treatment, thus, need more in-depth investigation. To more accurately establish the clinical utility of Dex in VAP cases, this study did a retrospective analysis of Intensive care unit (ICU) patient data specifically in VAP-diagnosed cases through the use of the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC-IV) dataset. Multivariate logistic regression and Kaplan-Meier survival analysis were utilized in this study in order to describe the interaction between administration of Dex and patient outcomes. These types of studies aim to provide novel information about VAP treatment, with the promise of enhancing both treatment efficacy and patient quality of life.

The data used in this study comes from the MIMIC-IV database (version 3.0). This database is extensive and includes de-identified records of over 65,000 intensive care unit admissions and over 200,000 visits to the emergency department from 2008 to 2022 at the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, Massachusetts. Both the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (Boston, Massachusetts) and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (Cambridge, Massachusetts) institutional review boards gave their approval for the creation of this database. The MIMIC-IV database has been made available to researcher Lin Bing, who has successfully completed all requirements and been issued a certification by the Cooperative Institutional Training Initiative (CITI) with the number 59,080,615. This study is in alignment with the ethical principles of the Declaration of Helsinki, and the de-identification procedures of the MIMIC-IV database ensure adherence to privacy protection laws, obviating the need for individual informed consent while fulfilling the requisite certification protocols.

Inclusion criteria: (1) individuals must be 18 years of age or older; (2) a confirmed diagnosis of VAP in the ICU, as classified by the International Classification of Diseases, Ninth and Tenth Editions (ICD-9 and ICD-10); (3) a minimum duration of ICU admission of 24 h; (4) the presence of comprehensive survival data. The criteria for exclusion are as follows: (1) multiple admissions to the ICU: in cases where a patient has several entries for ICU admissions, only the first admission will be taken into account for this study; (2) ICU stays that are less than 24 h in duration. Within the MIMIC-IV-3.0 database, individuals diagnosed with VAP are categorized using the following codes: “VAP” (code J95851), “VAP” (code 99731), and “Ventilation pneumonitis” (code 4957).

The process of data extraction utilizes PostgreSQL software (version 15.3) alongside Navicat Premium (version 16.3.2). The subsequent classifications of data have been obtained: (1) Demographic Information: Comprises age, gender, height, weight; (2) Clinical Data: Includes the Acute Physiology Score III (APSIII), SOFA score, Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score, administration of vasoactive medications(Including norepinephrine, epinephrine, phenylephrine, dopamine, and vasopressin) 22 , 23 . For ease of expression, all were converted to norepinephrine-equivalent doses (obtained using the materialized views provided by the database’s official website), denoted as NE in the text.), and the application of continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT); (3) Comorbidities: A detailed account of patient comorbidities including myocardial infarction (MI), congestive heart failure (CHF), hypertension, cerebrovascular disease (CAD), chronic pulmonary disease, liver disease, kidney disease, diabetes, and malignant tumors; (4) Key Indicators and Lab Findings: Documentation of the physiological parameters during the initial 24 h in intensive care unit admission is crucial. These include the lowest mean arterial pressure, heart rate (HR), respiratory rate (RR), maximum body temperature, and lowest oxygen saturation. A full assessment of the lab findings is also crucial, such as white blood cell count, percentage of lymphocytes and neutrophils, red cell distribution width, anion gap, level of lactic acid, partial pressure of carbon dioxide and oxygen, partial thromboplastin time, and biochemical parameters such as creatinine, blood urea nitrogen, and urine output. (5) Treatment information: whether patients received Dex therapy, including dosage and duration of Dex administration; dosage and duration of other sedative medications (propofol, midazolam); sedation scores (RASS, Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale); and antibiotic usage;6.Prognostic information: time of death, in-hospital mortality, duration of mechanical ventilation (MV-Los), length of hospital stay (Hospital-Los, days), ICU stay duration (ICU-Los, hours), and clinical status at a 3-month follow-up. For patients who are admitted to the ICU within a 24-h period, the most unfavorable value of the repeated laboratory indices is documented.

This study primarily assesses hospital mortality, with secondary attention to the 90-day survival rate. The data on mortality is derived from the “hospital expire flag” column within the “admissions” table of the MIMIC-IV database. The precise date of death is obtained from the “dod” column in the “patients” table, which synthesizes data from both hospital and state records. Data concerning the 3-month follow-up for all patients are also included. Additional outcome metrics encompass MV-Los, ICU stay duration, and overall hospital stay length.

In this study, some variables had a certain degree of missing data, with detailed data presented in Supplementary Table 1 . To ensure the integrity and functionality of the data, multiple imputation was performed utilizing the “mice” package 24 . Participants were classified into two distinct groups: individuals administered Dex were designated as the experimental group (DEX group), while those not receiving the treatment were allocated to the control group (Non-DEX group). The preliminary examination involved assessing the normal distribution of all continuous variables using the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. Data that adhered to a normal distribution were represented as mean ± standard deviation (M ± SD), while data that did not conform to this distribution were characterized by the median and interquartile range. Categorical variables were expressed as counts along with their corresponding percentages. The baseline characteristics among the groups were examined to discern any differences. Continuous variables that followed a normal distribution were analyzed using one-way ANOVA, whereas the Mann–Whitney U test was utilized for data that did not conform to normality. For categorical data, the assessment of differences was conducted utilizing the chi-square test. To investigate the correlation between Dex administration and in-hospital mortality, we employed both univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses, presenting odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals. The investigation encompassed two analytical frameworks: a basic model without adjustments and a multivariate model that incorporated various adjustments. The latter accounted for potential confounding factors identified by a p -value of less than 0.05 in univariate analysis, encompassing clinically significant variables and those associated with prognosis. Model 1 was the unadjusted model; Model 2 adjusted for age, gender, SOFA score, APSIII score, and Charlson comorbidity index (CCI) 25 . Model 3 incorporated adjustments for a broader set of variables including age, gender, clinical scores, comorbidities, and physiological and laboratory measures.Given that the database included patients from 2008 to 2022 with a substantial time span, we performed additional multivariable regression analyses stratified by different calendar years to account for potential temporal variations in treatment practices. Furthermore, we conducted subgroup analyses by categorizing patients according to quartile ranges of both Dex dosage and duration of administration to further evaluate their differential effects on clinical outcomes. Subgroup analysis was performed employing a hierarchical logistic regression model, stratifying participants by gender, age (≤ 60 years old and > 60 years old), SOFA score (≤ 8 points and > 8 points), use of vasoactive drugs, requirement for CRRT, and the presence of conditions such as malignant tumors, severe liver disease and kidney disease. Odds ratio (OR) and 95% confidence interval (CI) for each subgroup were computed. To evaluate interactions among subgroups, the likelihood ratio test was used, and a forest plot was generated. Additionally, Kaplan–Meier analysis facilitated the creation of cumulative survival curves for patients with follow-up periods extending beyond 90 days in both groups, and the log-rank test assessed differences in survival outcomes. Robustness Testing: To mitigate the influence of confounding variables and selection bias on the results of multivariate analyses, PSM was utilized with a caliper setting of 0.2 and a 1:1 matching ratio between the patient cohorts 26 . This matching included all variables specified in Model 3. Following matching, logistic regression analysis was conducted on the aligned dataset. Additionally, since the database does not document the exact onset or diagnosis time of VAP, making it difficult to determine whether Dex was administered before or after VAP development, we adopted a conservative analytical strategy. Specifically, we performed additional multivariable analyses by stratifying patients into two subgroups based on Dex initiation timing: within 48 h versus after 48 h of ICU admission, to verify the robustness of our findings. All statistical analyses were performed utilizing the software packages R version 3.4.3 and Stata/MP version 16.0. p < 0.05 were deemed statistically significant.

This study involved a total of 1766 patients diagnosed with VAP. The population was segmented into 905 individuals within the experimental group (DEX group) and 861 within the control group (Non-DEX group) (Fig. 1 ). The baseline characteristics are presented in Table 1 . The median age observed was 62.4 years, with males representing 65.9% (1164) of the entire cohort. Sedation-related outcomes: The two groups had comparable sedation depth (no statistically significant difference in RASS scores). No significant differences were observed between groups in midazolam utilization rate, duration of use, or dose per kilogram per hour (all comparisons P > 0.05). However, the DEX group demonstrated higher propofol utilization rates and longer duration of propofol administration.Antibiotic utilization patterns: The DEX group showed significantly higher usage rates of glycopeptides, cephalosporins, quinolones, nitroimidazoles, carbapenems, and macrolides. No between-group differences were observed for aminoglycosides, β-lactamase inhibitor combinations, or other antibiotic classes.In the analysis of vital signs and laboratory parameters, notable distinctions were identified among the groups across all metrics, with the exception of anion gap, HR, mean arterial pressure, blood glucose, platelet count, white blood cell count, APTT, urine output, and BUN. Variations in comorbid conditions, including CAD and malignant tumors, were observed among the groups. Outcome measures indicated a reduced in-hospital mortality rate in the DEX group, although this was accompanied by prolonged durations of hospitalization, ICU stays, and mechanical ventilation.

scirep__PMC12830661.pdf.h2: Univariate logistic analysis and multivariable logistic regression models
scirep__PMC12830661.pdf.text: Initially, a univariate logistic regression analysis was conducted to identify factors linked to in-hospital mortality among patients with VAP (Supplementary Table 2 ). Various factors, including gender, HR, mean arterial pressure, RR, SPO2 levels, dosage and duration of midazolam and propofol administration, chronic pulmonary disease, complications from diabetes, glucose, and platelet count, exhibited weak correlations with in-hospital mortality ( p ≥ 0.05). Although gender, platelet count, and blood glucose did not meet the statistical significance threshold, they were included as covariates in the multivariable analysis alongside all variables with p < 0.05, were incorporated as covariates in the multivariate analysis. The comprehensive list of covariates included age, gender, SOFA score, APSIII score, CCI, GCS score, use of vasoactive drugs, CRRT, RASS, weight, presence of malignant tumor, severe liver disease, MI, CHF, kidney disease, CAD, body temperature, anion gap, bicarbonate, BUN, creatinine, platelets, blood glucose, white blood cell count, coagulation time, urine volume, and mechanical ventilation duration. The results from the multivariate logistic regression analysis are presented in Table 2 . The unadjusted model (Model 1) revealed that Dex administration correlated with a decrease in in-hospital mortality among VAP patients [OR 0.55 (95% CI 0.44–0.69)]. Following adjustments for all confounding variables, the association continued to hold significance, as illustrated in Model 3, where the adjusted OR for in-hospital mortality in the DEX group was 0.62 (0.47–0.83).

The analysis, illustrated in Fig. 2 , identified a significant interaction between the administration of norepinephrine and the efficacy of Dex in reducing in-hospital mortality (interaction p -value = 0.036). Notably, Dex administration substantially decreased in-hospital mortality for patients receiving norepinephrine, with an OR of 0.41 compared to 0.56. Stratified analyses indicated that all subgroups, except those with concurrent MI, malignant tumors, and severe liver diseases—which showed an OR (95% CI) including 1—benefited from Dex treatment with a reduction in in-hospital mortality.Given that the database included patients from 2008 to 2022 with a substantial time span, we conducted additional multivariable regression analyses stratified by different calendar years to account for potential temporal variations in treatment practices. The results are presented in Table 3 . The findings demonstrate that when analyzed by three distinct chronological groupings, the DEX group consistently showed lower mortality rates (OR < 1, p < 0.05) across all time periods. Furthermore, all P-values for interaction exceeded 0.05, indicating no significant effect modification by time period on the association between Dex and mortality.

Throughout this study, comprehensive 90-day survival data were available for all participants. Survival curves were constructed to provide a clear visual representation of the survival trends over time for these patients. As illustrated in Fig. 3 , the survival curves for the DEX group (Dex = 1) and the Non-DEX group (Dex = 0) exhibited a significant divergence, with the DEX group showing markedly extended survival durations. The observed difference reached statistical significance ( p < 0.001), highlighting the possible survival advantages of Dex in patients with VAP.

scirep__PMC12830661.pdf.h2: Impact of Dex dosage and duration on outcomes
scirep__PMC12830661.pdf.text: We stratified patients by quartile ranges of Dex dosage and duration of administration to evaluate their effects on in-hospital mortality, as shown in Table 4 . Duration of Dex administration: Groups with Dex duration < 153.5 h (all three lower quartiles) showed significantly lower in-hospital mortality ( P < 0.05).Dex dosage: The two middle dosage groups (0.353–0.962 mcg/kg/h) demonstrated significantly reduced in-hospital mortality ( P < 0.05).Trend analysis: Both dosage and duration exhibited statistically significant trends ( P for trend < 0.05), indicating a consistent association between Dex use and lower in-hospital mortality.

To rigorously control for confounding variables in this study, PSM was employed for both patient groups. The caliper was set at 0.2, and the matching ratio was maintained at 1:1. The matching included all variables outlined in Model 3. After implementing PSM, 559 pairs of patients were successfully matched, totaling 1118 individuals 27 . The baseline characteristics of these patients are detailed in Table 5 . Post-matching, an assessment of the baseline data—encompassing demographic information, disease severity, RASS scores, vital signs, laboratory tests, and comorbidity profiles—demonstrated effective equivalence between the two groups, with no significant differences in these baseline characteristics (all p values > 0.05). Outcome measures revealed distinctive results for the DEX group, which exhibited a lower in-hospital mortality rate but longer durations of mechanical ventilation compared to the Non-DEX group. Subsequent analyses, including univariate and multivariate regression on the matched dataset, are summarized in Table 6 . These analyses showed that Dex significantly lowered in-hospital mortality [OR 0.59 (95%CI 0.42–0.83)]. Additionally, as the database did not label the specific onset time and diagnosis time of ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP), it was challenging to distinguish whether Dex was administered before or after the occurrence of VAP. A conservative analytical strategy was therefore adopted. Patients were grouped based on whether Dex was initiated within 48 h or after 48 h of ICU admission. Multivariate analysis was then conducted again, and the results are presented in Table 7 . Compared with the Non-DEX group, the use of Dex, whether initiated within 48 h or after 48 h of ICU admission, was associated with a lower in-hospital mortality rate (OR < 1, p < 0.05). Moreover, the p-value for trend in the trend test was less than 0.05, indicating that the results were robust and reliable.

This MIMIC-IV database retrospective study illustrates that Dex administration is linked with reduced mortality among VAP inpatients during their in-hospital stay. When compared with non-Dex-treated individuals, Dex-treated individuals had a lower in-hospital mortality rate, with an OR of 0.62 (95% CI 0.47–0.83), and with significantly extended survival durations. This correlation remained consistent across subgroup analyses and propensity score matching (PSM) analysis, indicating the robustness of the results. However, the DEX group had longer durations of mechanical ventilation and hospital stay. which might be attributable to the relatively more severe condition of patients in this group, as evidenced by higher Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) scores and Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation III (APSIII) scores, a greater proportion of patients requiring norepinephrine support and continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT), and lower Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) scores. Subgroup analyses revealed that except for patients with comorbid myocardial infarction, malignant tumors, or severe liver diseases, all other subgroups benefited from Dex treatment in terms of reduced in-hospital mortality. As seen from the baseline table, the DEX group had more extensive use of broad-spectrum antibiotics (such as carbapenems, glycopeptides, third-generation cephalosporins, etc.) 28 . In contrast, the Non-DEX group had a narrower spectrum of antibiotic use, with relatively more quinolones (which may reflect a higher proportion of community-acquired infections). Despite the DEX group exhibiting the following higher-risk characteristics: more severe illness (higher Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) scores, greater use of norepinephrine (NE)) and a heavier infectious burden (more extensive use of broad-spectrum antibiotics), the in-hospital mortality rate in this group was still significantly lower. This finding: reinforces the protective effect of Dex—even in more critically ill patients, Dex can significantly reduce mortality. It suggests that the benefits of Dex may extend beyond its mere sedative effects—its anti-inflammatory, organ-protective, and other mechanisms may be particularly crucial for patients with severe infections. The Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale (RASS) is used as a tool to assess the depth of sedation. The absence of a statistically significant difference in RASS scores between the two groups indicates that the levels of sedation were similar. However, the mortality rate in the DEX group was significantly lower than that in the Non-DEX group (18.7% vs. 29.5%). This phenomenon may be related to the anti-inflammatory and lung-protective effects of Dex. Under a personalized sedation strategy aimed at achieving mild sedation, the suppression of respiratory and circulatory functions can be minimized while maintaining patient comfort and cooperation. By implementing a personalized sedation strategy and using Dex, the incidence of complications in patients with ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) can be reduced. For example, it can decrease the occurrence of psychiatric symptoms such as delirium and agitation, as well as lower the risk of accidental extubation. The occurrence of these complications not only affects the treatment efficacy and prognosis of patients but also increases healthcare costs and nursing burdens. The temporal stability analysis in Table 5 demonstrated consistent clinical benefits of Dex across all three time-stratified models (2008–2016/2017–2022, 2008–2013/2014–2022, and 2008–2013/2017–2022), with significantly lower in-hospital mortality in the DEX group versus Non-DEX controls (all P < 0.05). The non-significant interaction terms (all P for interaction > 0.05: 0.954/0.256/0.445) confirmed the temporal consistency of Dex’s therapeutic benefits.These findings robustly validate the sustained clinical efficacy of Dex across different treatment eras. Through rigorous time-stratified analyses, this study provides high-level evidence supporting the enduring clinical value of Dex over a 15-year span, establishing its long-term utility in critical care medicine. In the subgroup analysis of Dex dosage and duration, all groups with Dex duration < 153.5 h showed significantly reduced mortality ( P < 0.05). However, as the duration of use increased, the protective effect showed a trend of weakening. The 153.5-h mark may represent a critical turning point, as the group with a duration ≥ 153.5 h ( P = 0.174) lost statistical significance. In the dose-response relationship analysis, the dose range of 0.353–0.962 mcg/kg/h exhibited the strongest protective effect (OR 0.54–0.57, P < 0.05). It is recommended to control the Dex dosage within the range of 0.353–0.962 mcg/kg/h and limit the duration of use to no more than 153.5 h (approximately 6.5 days), as exceeding these limits may diminish clinical benefits. Therefore, a moderate dose of Dex, achieving an optimal balance between sedation depth, anti-inflammatory effects, and adverse reactions, may confer significant benefits by reducing in-hospital mortality. Given the absence of documented VAP onset/diagnosis times in the database, we implemented a conservative analytical approach by stratifying patients based on Dex initiation timing (≤ 48 h vs. >48 h after ICU admission). Key findings from this time-stratified analysis include: the early-use group (≤ 48 h) demonstrated an absolute reduction in mortality of 15.4% (from 29.5% to 14.1%), while the late-use group (> 48 h) showed an absolute reduction of 9.5% (from 29.5% to 20%). Potential mechanisms: Preemptive anti-inflammatory effects (blocking cytokine cascades)Reduction of early sedation-related complications.Persistent benefits may derive from: its ability to block ongoing anti-sympathetic storm effects, its immunomodulatory actions, and indirect benefits derived from preventing delirium, among other factors.

VAP occurs in patients more than 48 h after mechanical ventilation via tracheal intubation or tracheotomy. The pathogenesis of VAP involves two main mechanisms: firstly, volume trauma from ventilation-related airway pressure can cause diffuse damage to the alveolar-capillary membrane and increase its permeability 29 , secondly, the aggressive mechanical stretching by the ventilator triggers the release of inflammatory mediators from lung resident cells, which promotes the transcription and expression of pro-inflammatory factors, initiating an inflammatory cascade that results in lung injury 30 . Consequently, the primary treatment strategies for VAP focus on preventive measures, along with empirical anti-inflammatory therapies, anti-infection approaches, and alveolar lavage via fiber bronchoscopy. Recent studies have highlighted the pulmonary protective effects of Dex in various contexts of lung injury 31 , including its influence on pulmonary vascular contraction mechanisms, mitigation of ischemia-reperfusion injury, and modulation of inflammatory cytokine release. As an α(2)-adrenergic receptor agonist, Dex has been shown to reduce the synthesis of inflammatory mediators in the body and inhibit the activation of the TLRs/NF-κB signal transduction 32 , proving effective in VAP management. Through increased oxidative stress response, Dex significantly increases oxygenation in the lung and maintains lung function, which, in addition to minimizing the frequency of multiple organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS) in patients, results in reduced in-hospital mortality.

Currently, clinical investigations into Dex for VAP suggest its potential to reduce inflammatory mediator levels, improve respiratory mechanics, and enhance pulmonary oxygenation in the early stages of the condition. These mechanisms may contribute to lung protection and potentially decrease the incidence of MODS. However, these studies often lack consideration of clinical endpoint indicators and are constrained by small sample sizes, which casts uncertainty on whether Dex truly enhances VAP prognosis 33 , 34 . In contrast, the present study addresses these gaps by focusing specifically on the high-risk VAP population and leveraging a large, real-world cohort from the authoritative MIMIC-IV database. To our knowledge, this is the first study to comprehensively assess the association between Dex and clinically pivotal outcomes—specifically in-hospital mortality and survival time—in VAP patients, while rigorously adjusting for numerous confounding factors. Furthermore, our work is pioneering in its extensive subgroup and sensitivity analyses, which reinforce the robustness of the findings. Collectively, our results corroborate that Dex may serve as a protective factor in VAP, providing a foundational evidence base for future prospective studies aimed at optimizing its use in this vulnerable patient group. Despite these strengths, the study is not without its limitations: (1) The retrospective nature of the study limits the ability to establish causality and may introduce selection bias. For instance, the decision to administer Dex may be influenced by clinical factors such as sedation requirements and hemodynamic stability, and physician preference, which could confound the observed outcomes. Additionally, due to the lack of chest computed tomography (CT) images in the database, we could not conduct imaging scoring for pneumonia, which is known to correlate with prognosis; (2) The inclusion of VAP patients relied on diagnostic codes, which may not have captured all cases and could be subject to misclassification. Furthermore, the definition of VAP has evolved over time, which may affect the consistency of the diagnosis across the study period. However, due to the inherent structure of the MIMIC database, beyond relying on diagnostic codes, it was not feasible to extract additional clinical data to determine whether patients had concurrent VAP; (3) Significant data loss led to the exclusion of some prognostically important indicators such as hemoglobin, blood lactic acid, oxygenation index, electrolytes, and albumin levels, where the missing data rate was over 20%. Substantial missing data for certain prognostic indicators may affect the validity of our conclusions, despite our use of multiple imputation methods.

Our study’s reliance on diagnostic codes for VAP case identification underscores the need for more rigorous validation in future research. To address this and other complexities of VAP, subsequent investigations should focus on: Validation through Prospective Trials: Conducting prospective, multicenter randomized controlled trials that employ standardized, clinical VAP diagnostic criteria (rather than administrative codes) to conclusively validate the association between Dex and patient outcomes. Dosage Optimization: Establishing the specific and optimal dosage and timing of Dex administration in critically ill patients with VAP. Exploration of Synergy: Investigating the potential for synergistic effects when Dex is combined with other therapeutic strategies, such as novel antimicrobials or immunomodulators, to develop a more comprehensive management approach.

Based on our findings, Dex appears to reduce in-hospital mortality and extend survival times in VAP patients. Consequently, additional clinical trials are warranted to provide more conclusive evidence regarding its efficacy in improving clinical outcomes for these patients.

scirep__PMC12834942.pdf.text: This study introduces a novel evaluation framework that combines a space-time graph diffusion model (STG-DM) and federated contrastive learning (FedCL) to address collaborative optimization challenges in cross-school education evaluation. This integration enables the creation of a thermodynamically driven space-time diffusion equation and an adaptive graph convolution mechanism, facilitating accurate modeling of the space-time evolution of multimodal educational behaviors. It effectively overcomes the shortcomings of traditional methods, which often suffer from local overfitting and dynamic correlation modeling failures due to data silos. The graph diffusion operator, constrained by non-equilibrium thermodynamic principles, has proven to enhance the prediction accuracy of cross-regional education strategies, reducing the average absolute error (MAE) by 18.7% compared to conventional space-time models. In the context of heterogeneous data distribution across 30 universities, the system successfully reduces the privacy leakage risk (ε) to below 1.5, while simultaneously achieving balanced optimization of cross-school model generalization performance. The lightweight evaluation system developed includes a multimodal real-time analysis engine that enables space-time heatmap rendering and collaborative decision-making for 100,000-level nodes, with a system response delay of less than two seconds. This provides education managers with efficient and reliable data intelligence tools. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1038/s41598-025-33376-x. Keywords: Evaluation system, Cross-institutional evaluation, Graph diffusion model, Federated contrastive learning, Multimodal analysis Subject terms: Engineering, Mathematics and computing

As higher education institutions increasingly digitize their educational frameworks, cross-institutional collaborative assessment has become crucial for improving teaching quality. However, the conflict between multi-institutional data sharing and privacy protection is escalating 1 . Currently, about 78% of universities operate independent evaluation systems, leading to severe data silos that obscure correlations between cross-institutional educational behaviors and outcomes 2 . Mainstream assessment methods over-rely on static indicators such as course completion rates and exam scores, failing to reflect the dynamic nature of teacher–student interactions 3 . Although the traditional Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) allows weight quantification, it struggles to incorporate fluid factors like classroom atmosphere and regional cultural differences 4 . Moreover, integration techniques for multi-source data—such as video, text, and administrative records—remain underdeveloped; approximately 63% of evaluation systems support only single-mode analysis 5 . These limitations prevent current approaches from meeting modern education’s demands for precision, collaboration, and intelligence. In recent years, federated learning has introduced innovative solutions for data privacy, yet model generalization across institutions remains challenging. For example, non-IID data can induce prediction biases of up to 22% in global models across heterogeneous populations 6 . While spatio-temporal graph models are capable of capturing complex relational patterns, their high computational complexity hinders practical deployment. A novel end-to-end federated comparative learning model has been proposed for cross-domain recommendation, helping mitigate bias between global and local models 7 . Another approach introduces a bi-heterogeneous three-stage coupled network with multivariate feature-aware learning, which adapts to evolving patterns by integrating low-, mid-, and high-level feature extraction to improve multi-feature perception and prediction accuracy 8 . Thus, there is an urgent need to develop an evaluation framework that reconciles privacy preservation, dynamic modeling, and computational efficiency. The core challenge in cross-institutional educational assessment lies in balancing data privacy with model efficacy. Data silos across institutions increase the risk of local model overfitting. Conventional federated aggregation strategies such as FedAvg can reduce global model accuracy by 14%–18% under non-IID data distributions 9 , 10 . Additionally, educational behaviors exhibit strong spatio-temporal dependencies—such as regional cultural impacts on instructional strategies—which conventional temporal models like LSTM fail to adequately capture across spatial nodes 11 . Experiments indicate that single-time-series models yield a 26% higher RMSE compared to spatio-temporal fusion models in cross-regional evaluations 12 . Multimodal data fusion introduces further complexity. Educational outcomes are influenced by numerous factors, including teaching behavior (video), student feedback (text), and administrative policies (structured data). Current fusion techniques often rely on simple feature concatenation, leading to information loss of up to 35% 13 . Privacy mechanisms like differential noise injection may also impair model sensitivity to critical features; for instance, noise addition in joint models has been shown to reduce the F1 score by 9.3% in sentiment classification tasks 14 . Therefore, it is essential to design adaptive noise injection and feature enhancement strategies that reconcile privacy constraints with model robustness. In the domain of spatio-temporal graph models, the ST-GCN model captures spatial correlations by fixing the topological structure 15 . However, this structure struggles to adapt to dynamic policy interventions during the propagation of educational behaviors. While ConvNeXt-V2 aims to enhance visual representations through masked modeling, its inherent Euclidean space assumption fundamentally conflicts with the manifold characteristics of educational data 16 , 17 . In federated learning scenarios, Fed Avg’s homogeneous aggregation method generates up to 22% prediction bias when handling cross-school non-IID data 18 . Although FedProx employs regularization to constrain client drift 19 , it fails to address cross-modal knowledge alignment issues 20 . In thermodynamic modeling, the equilibrium diffusion hypothesis fails to explain abrupt phenomena triggered by regional cultural impedance factors, such as the sixth-month curriculum adjustment at the Beijing campus 21 . Spatio-temporal Graph Neural Networks (STGNNs) have demonstrated their modelling capabilities for dynamic correlations across domains such as transportation and meteorology. ST-GCN and DCRNN pioneered the integration of graph diffusion processes with convolutional operations; however, their default static topology and node homogeneity render them ill-suited to accommodate rapid topological shifts in educational settings arising from policy or cultural variations. DGT-MTL enhances traffic prediction robustness through a multi-task dynamic graph Transformer, with its adaptive multi-task learning module capable of revealing implicit associations and dynamic relationships between road segments 22 . FDGNN further proposes decoupled contrastive objectives to prevent sensitive attribute leakage, achieving fair representation 23 . Unlike the aforementioned approaches, this study’s FedCL-STGDM decouples contrastive learning across temporal and spatial domains. It constructs cross-calibration samples using course semantics and generates negative samples through discipline-heterogeneous methods. Furthermore, it extends dynamic graph transformations to policy-triggered topological evolution, employing a non-equilibrium thermodynamic diffusion operator for adaptive edge weight adjustment. Complemented by Stiefel manifold projection for lightweight aggregation, it achieves 38% reduced communication with ε ≤ 1.5. This pioneering approach unites communication efficiency and privacy protection, enabling cross-institutional educational assessment through integrated dynamic STGNN and privacy-aware contrastive learning. This study pioneers the introduction of nonlinear response terms, enabling the diffusion coefficient matrix to dynamically adapt to each campus’s unique characteristics. In the field of fourth-order tensor theory, traditional third-order modeling results in up to 35% loss of cross-modal mutual information. This study pioneers the construction of a pattern interaction matrix, encoding the correlations among video, text, and management records into higher-order tensors via fourth-order convolutional kernels. This approach achieves a cross-modal mutual information value of 3.05 ± 0.35 at the Guangzhou campus. Recent studies have further expanded the technical path of federated learning and spatio-temporal modelling. For example, one study proposed a joint communication optimisation strategy based on the attention mechanism, which significantly reduces the bandwidth overhead of cross-device collaboration 24 ; scholars combined LSTM and GRU to capture the range of long and short information in population sequences to mitigate the limitations of previous approaches 25 ; and another deployed diffusion models into a federated learning framework to achieve optimal privacy preservation and performance for heterogeneous data 26 . In this study, the advanced concepts of the above achievements are borrowed and integrated in the design of STG-DM and FedCL frameworks, especially in the optimisation of the joint aggregation efficiency and multimodal feature extraction, which are innovatively explored. This system integrates a Spatio-Temporal Graph Diffusion Model (STG-DM) with Federated Contrastive Learning (Fed CL) to address key limitations in data privacy, dynamic modeling, and system efficiency. The STG-DM model, inspired by thermodynamic diffusion theory, employs spatio-temporal attention mechanisms and adaptive graph convolutions to enhance dynamic modeling of cross-regional educational behaviors. Experiments show it reduces mean absolute error (MAE) by 18.7% over conventional spatio-temporal models under heterogeneous data conditions 27 . Additionally, a hierarchical Fed CL framework utilizing dynamic weight aggregation and local knowledge distillation effectively mitigates the generalization bottleneck caused by multi-university data silos. In cross-domain tests involving 30 universities, this approach increased global evaluation accuracy by 12.5% while maintaining privacy leakage risk (ε) below 1.5, achieving an optimal balance between privacy and performance 28 . For practical application, a lightweight evaluation system incorporating a multimodal visualization engine and a real-time decision-making module was developed. It supports spatio-temporal heatmap analysis, risk alerts, and cross-institutional interventions for over 100,000 samples, with system response latency under 2 s, offering administrators an efficient and reliable data intelligence tool 29 , 30 . As illustrated in Fig. 1 , the system not only bridges technical gaps in dynamic association modeling and privacy-preserving collaborative computing but also provides a theoretical and engineering foundation for building secure educational assessment frameworks. This study addresses the problem of Spatio-Temporal Predictive Evaluation for Cross-Institutional Education. Formally, the task can be defined as follows: Input: At any time step t , the input consists of multimodal data from N universities, denoted as , where: is the spatio-temporal graph for university , with nodes representing classrooms/teachers and edges representing interaction relationships. is the node feature matrix, encompassing features like teaching behavior entropy and teacher-student interaction frequency. is the multivariate time series of management records. Output: The model aims to predict future educational outcomes (e.g., comprehensive evaluation scores) for each university over a future time horizon . Objective: The goal is to learn a global predictive model under the federated learning constraint, where the raw data never leaves each local institution . The model must simultaneously: Achieve high prediction accuracy by capturing complex spatio-temporal dependencies. Preserve data privacy against potential leakage from shared model updates. Maintain robustness against heterogeneous (non-IID) data distributions across institutions. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: A non-equilibrium ST graph diffusion model (STG-DM) that reduces MAE by 18.7% vs. best baseline. A hierarchical federated contrastive learning (FedCL) module that improves global accuracy by 12.5% while keeping ε < 1.5. A lightweight evaluation system that renders 100 k-node heat-maps within 2s. Extensive experiments on the real-world CSED−24 dataset and a 30-university deployment. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section “ Method design ” introduces the methodology, including cross-school education data modeling, the spatio-temporal graph diffusion model (STG-DM), and the federated contrastive learning (FedCL) framework. Section “ Method overview and framework ” details the system implementation and experimental setup, including dataset description, model configurations, and performance evaluation. Section “ Educational adaptation of STGNN principles ” presents the application and verification of the proposed framework in a real-world case study. Section “ Cross school education data modeling ” discusses the implications and limitations of the study, and Sect. “ Space-time alignment and feature extraction ” concludes the paper with future research directions.

To tackle the problem defined in Sect. “ Introduction ”, we propose the Fed CL-STGDM framework, whose components are specifically designed to address the core challenges: Challenge A: Modeling Dynamic Spatio-Temporal Dependencies in Educational Behaviors. Solution: We design the Spatio-Temporal Graph Diffusion Model (STG-DM) (Sect. “ Educational adaptation of STGNN principles ”). Its thermodynamic diffusion equations and adaptive graph convolutions are tailored to capture the non-linear evolution of interactions and policy impacts across the educational graph. 2) Challenge B: Enabling Collaborative Learning under Privacy and Data Heterogeneity Constraints. Solution: We introduce a Federated Contrastive Learning (FedCL) scheme (Sect. “ Cross school education data modeling ”). This component uses dynamic weight aggregation and local knowledge distillation to align models from different institutions without sharing raw data, thereby mitigating the effects of data silos and non-IID distributions. 3) Challenge C: Fusing Multimodal Educational Data. Solution: We construct a Cross-school Education Data Model (Sect. “ Method overview and framework ”) based on high-order tensor decomposition and manifold embedding, which provides a unified representation for heterogeneous features (video, text, records) as inputs to the STG-DM. The interplay of these components ensures that our framework directly targets the requirements of the defined predictive evaluation task. The schematic diagram of the modelling framework is shown in Fig. 2 .

Although the core mechanisms of Spatio-Temporal Graph Neural Networks (STGNNs) have been extensively studied in fields such as traffic forecasting and human behavior modeling, their direct application to education remains challenging. We hereby elucidate how the proposed framework uniquely adapts STGNN principles to modeling educational processes: Domain-specific graph construction. Unlike physical-space graphs (e.g., road networks), the graph in our study represents instructional relationships and learning-behavior dependencies. Nodes correspond to students’ learning states or learning activities, while edges represent pedagogical correlations such as prerequisite knowledge, learning-behavior co-occurrence, or knowledge-concept transition probability. This educational graph structure embeds explicit semantic information aligned with instructional theory. Educationally meaningful temporal dynamics. The temporal patterns modeled by STGNN are not generic time correlations but represent learning progression trajectories. Our temporal module is designed to capture phenomena such as forgetting curves, periodic learning cycles, and the accumulation of cognitive load—features that differ significantly from STGNN applications in other domains. Pedagogically interpretable feature aggregation. During spatial–temporal message passing, aggregated features reflect how multiple learning behaviors jointly influence a learner’s performance or engagement. We constrain the aggregation rules to maintain interpretability, enabling educators to understand which behavioral signals contribute to observed outcomes. Task-specific educational optimization. Unlike traditional STGNN objectives, our loss function incorporates indicators that reflect instructional performance, such as mastery progression, engagement variation, and learning-path efficiency. This aligns the model with educational goals rather than generic prediction accuracy. These domain-driven adaptations ensure that the proposed method is not merely a direct reuse of standard STGNN concepts but an education-centered redesign that captures the unique dynamics of real-world learning environments.

Traditional Euclidean coordinates (e.g. latitude and longitude) or complex representations have inherent limitations in modelling the spatio-temporal dynamics of educational behaviour. They have difficulty dealing uniformly with rotations (e.g., orientation relationships between different school districts) and temporal evolution in three-dimensional space and cannot naturally characterize complex interactions between multimodal features. For this reason, we introduce quaternion spatio-temporal coding. In contrast to the simple representation, quaternions (of the form ) provides a compact, non-commutative algebraic framework capable of uniformly representing rotations and translations in three-dimensional space, which is more consistent with the geometrical properties of educational strategies propagating through physical space and abstract feature space. Specifically, as shown in Eq. ( 3 ), we map geographic locations to quaternion spaces, thereby embedding spatial relationships into a learnable representation of the model. Further, in order to effectively fuse the spatio-temporal features encoded by quaternions with those of other modalities (e.g., text, video), we employ Clifford algebra operations. As shown in Eq. ( 4 ), this operation allows us to perform implicit multiplication and addition operations on features from different manifolds (e.g., spatio-temporal manifolds, textual-semantic manifolds) in a unified algebraic system, which preserves the geometric structure of the modalities and facilitates deeper interactions between them than simply splicing them together and feeding them into a fully connected network. The utility of this higher-order representation is ultimately validated by its ability to enhance cross-modal synergy. To ensure reproducibility, we specify the core network architectures. The STG-DM encoder consists of a two-layer adaptive graph convolution with hidden dimensions of [64, 128], followed by a spatio-temporal attention layer (ASTA, Eq. 12 ) with 8 attention heads. The extracted features are then processed by a temporal decoder comprising a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) with a hidden size of 256 and a linear output layer. The FedCL framework’s projection heads, used for contrastive learning, are implemented as a 3-layer Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) with dimensions [feature_dim, 512, 256, 128] and ReLU activation. This projects client features into a common latent space for comparison. All models were implemented in PyTorch 1.12.1 and trained on a server with NVIDIA A100 GPUs.

This study proposes a distributed intelligent system for cross-school education evaluation, designed and implemented based on the theoretical framework of the Space-Time Graph Diffusion Model (STG-DM) and Federated Comparative Learning (Fed CL). In constructing the CSED−24 dataset, our research team gathered classroom surveillance videos from 30 universities using multimodal fusion technology. Specifically, we utilized the Hikvision DS−2CD3T86 camera, which was sampled at 5 frames per second and adjusted to a resolution of 1280 × 720. Additionally, we collected student course feedback texts, totaling 23,000 instances. These were gathered via a questionnaire network platform, with an average text length of 58.3 characters, as well as structured management records exported from the educational administration system. These records comprised 12 types of fields including attendance and grades. For video preprocessing, we first sparsified the original 5 fps 1280 × 720 H.264 stream by retaining one key frame out of every three. We then applied YOLOv5m-face (confidence threshold = 0.65, NMS = 0.45) to detect teacher and student bounding-boxes, discarding boxes whose area < 1% of the frame. A TSN backbone extracted an 8-D behaviour vector (hand-raising, head-lowering, writing, etc.). Any segment with action entropy < 0.15 or confidence fluctuation > ± 0.25 for eight consecutive frames was regarded as an abnormal silence clip and removed. Each lecture was finally represented by a fixed-length sequence of L v = 150 frames; sequences shorter than 150 frames were zero-padded at the tail, whereas longer ones were down-sampled uniformly to guarantee identical tensor size across campuses. Textual feedback was first tokenised and POS-tagged by Harbin-IT LTP 4.1. Stop-words were removed using the Harbin extended list (1 893 words) together with any token shorter than two characters. We built an education-specific sentiment dictionary of 1 847 entries (892 positive, 955 negative) and obtained 1 024-dimensional sentence embeddings via RoBERTa-wwm-ext. To handle length variance, we set a maximum length of 64 tokens; shorter posts were padded with [PAD], and longer ones were head-and-tail truncated (first 48 + last 16 tokens), yielding a uniform input tensor of size N ×64 × 1024. Data cleansing standards were set as follows: noise records containing fewer than 15 characters or exhibiting sentiment polarity variability exceeding 3.0 were removed. For missing values, the administrative records comprised 12 fields (attendance rate, grades, assignment submission rate, etc.). We first calculated the proportion of missing values grouped by course-class-week. Fields with less than 5% missing values were imputed using linear interpolation; the remaining fields were processed via MissForest. All numerical features undergo Z-score standardisation, whilst categorical variables are target-coded to mitigate the high cardinality effect. The final cleaned dataset is organised into a 12 × 24-hour tensor, with remaining hourly-level missing values imputed via forward filling to preserve temporal continuity. This yielded a comprehensive multimodal dataset encompassing video behaviour matrices (25 dimensions per sample), textual sentiment vectors (1024 dimensions per sample), and management feature tensors (12 × 24 dimensions). Following data cleansing, the dataset comprised 187,000 valid samples with a purity rate of 93.6%. This significant efficiency difference strongly suggests a negative correlation between the regional cultural resistance factor and the speed of model convergence. To quantitatively verify this observation, we calculated the Pearson correlation coefficients between the cultural resistance factor and the corresponding convergence period for the six regions. The results of the analyses show a strong negative correlation ( r =−0.89, p < 0.02). This means that the higher the cultural resistance factor, the longer it takes for the model to reach convergence. There is a clear mechanistic explanation for this finding: higher cultural resistance factors (e.g. 0.183 in Chengdu) reflect the fact that educational behaviors in the region are more frequently subject to dynamic policy interventions, resulting in a more noisy and uncertain local data distribution. In a federated learning framework, this directly translates into greater client drift, which in turn requires more communication rounds to coordinate model updates on different clients, and ultimately manifests itself in longer convergence times. On the contrary, regions with low cultural resistance factors like Guangzhou, where the data distribution is relatively stable, have a smoother and more efficient federated optimisation process. This analysis not only confirms the effectiveness of the cultural resistance factor as a quantitative indicator of regional heterogeneity, but also provides a key basis for predicting and optimizing cross-regional federated learning deployments in practice: for regions with high resistance factors, more aggressive client regularization or dynamically weighted aggregation strategies may be required to alleviate convergence bottlenecks. These strategies encompassed federated aggregation frequency, privacy budget ε (as delineated in Eq. 12 ), and resource scheduling cycle. The experimental duration spanned three months, during which data was collected from 500 courses across 20 universities. The findings of this research are presented in Table 17 . The data suggests that the adaptive aggregation strategy model yields the highest level of accuracy; however, it presents a response delay of 2150 ms. This necessitates a balance between real-time performance and precision. The low-frequency aggregation poses the least risk for privacy leakage, yet it offers a resource utilization rate of only 78.9%, suggesting the need for dynamic adjustments to the federated aggregation frequency. The fixed privacy budget (ε=1.5) effectively balances resource utilization (88.2%) with model accuracy (0.848), making it optimal for long-term deployment. Within the context of user behavior analysis, Fig. 10 demonstrates that the frequency of teaching reflection has a strong positive correlation with model accuracy. This confirms the beneficial influence of real-time warning modules on teaching optimization. Conversely, the number of resource searches exhibits a negative correlation with response latency. This suggests an area for system improvement in terms of caching strategy. Furthermore, the initiation of cross-school collaborations shows a positive correlation with resource consumption. Consequently, it is imperative to strike a balance between the advantages of collaboration and the additional hardware load induced.

The cross-school education assessment system proposed in this study, which is based on the spatio-temporal graph diffusion model (STG-DM) and federated contrastive learning (Fed CL), has yielded significant results in terms of data privacy protection, dynamic spatio-temporal modeling, and model generalization capabilities. Firstly, from a theoretical innovation standpoint, the STG-DM enables high-precision modeling of the spatio-temporal evolution of educational behavior via thermodynamically driven diffusion equations and adaptive spatio-temporal attention mechanisms. This approach effectively addresses the issue of local overfitting caused by the failure of dynamic association modeling in traditional methods in data silo scenarios, thereby reducing the mean absolute error (MAE) by 18.7%. Secondly, the Fed CL framework adeptly mitigates the model generalization bottleneck induced by data silos across multiple schools through the utilization of dynamic weight aggregation and local knowledge distillation strategies. In cross-domain testing, it enhances the global evaluation accuracy by 12.5% and stringently controls the privacy leakage risk (ε) within 1.5, thereby achieving a balanced optimization of privacy protection and model performance. This study pioneers the application of thermodynamic diffusion principles to education spatio-temporal modeling, culminating in the development of a lightweight evaluation system with independent intellectual property rights. This novel system facilitates real-time spatio-temporal analysis of 100,000 nodes, offering a comprehensive visualization of educational outcomes via a multi-scale visualization engine. When contrasted with traditional federated learning frameworks, our dynamic aggregation strategy enhances model training efficiency by approximately 40%, demonstrating stable convergence characteristics even under extreme data distribution scenarios. Furthermore, the privacy protection layer strategically combines Rényi differential privacy and gradient truncation technology. This ensures strict adherence to privacy budget constraints while maintaining an acceptable level of model utility loss. From an operational standpoint, the implementation at Chengdu D School illustrates that the data-driven evaluation model can expedite the decision-making process from a traditionally experience-driven six months to a real-time response, with a system warning delay of less than two seconds and a strategy iteration cycle of seven days. Following the implementation of the Fed CL-STGDM system, a correlative improvement of 37% in evaluation accuracy was observed at Chengdu D School. While this substantial gain is temporally associated with the system’s deployment and aligns with its intended functionality, we acknowledge that the observational nature of this case study limits definitive causal attribution. To strengthen the validity of this finding, future work should employ controlled A/B testing. However, the initial resistance to change observed at Beijing University A underscores the necessity for a transitional framework that combines both data and experience in decision-making. This approach entails first fine-tuning the weights of experience-based metrics using data during the preliminary stages, and then gradually shifting towards fully data-driven decision-making through federated collaboration in subsequent phases. A pilot study conducted at Shijiazhuang University B using this hybrid model yielded promising results, with the model’s accuracy reaching 82.1%, marking a 19.5% improvement over purely experience-based models. It is important to address the methodological context of this real-world verification. The deployment of the Fed CL-STGDM system across the university alliance was a strategic decision, precluding the establishment of a randomized control group for a classical A/B test. Consequently, the performance comparisons presented here are primarily observational. To mitigate the inherent limitations of this design and bolster the claim of the system’s effectiveness, we pursued two strategies: First, we compared the trajectory of Chengdu D School against the static. experience-driven approach of Beijing A School, demonstrating a significant performance gap that emerged concurrently with our system’s adoption. Second, and more critically, the internal ablation studies and controlled laboratory experiments on the CSED−24 dataset provide robust, controlled evidence for the mechanistic superiority of the Fed CL-STGDM framework. The strong performance observed in the field study is consistent with these controlled experimental results, suggesting that the observed improvements are likely driven by the implemented system. Despite the high technical complexity of STG-DM and FedCL framework, the system has effectively transformed from ‘technical indicators’ to ‘management insights’ through multi-level visualisation and semantic transformation mechanisms. For example, in Chengdu, School D, the system identified ‘2−4pm as an inefficient time for interaction’ and quickly adjusted the course schedule to increase student engagement by 18%. This shows that by providing an intuitive, actionable feedback interface, education administrators can make efficient decisions without having to deeply understand the mechanics of the model. In the future, we will further introduce interpretable AI techniques, such as feature importance attribution, to enhance the trust and acceptance of the model output on the management side. Although the STG-DM with FedCL framework proposed in this study performs well in cross-school educational assessment, it still has several limitations. First, the model is highly dependent on high-quality multimodal data. In the data collection stage, if the video quality is low, the text sentiment labelling is inconsistent or the administrative records are missing, it will directly affect the accuracy of spatio-temporal alignment and feature fusion. For example, in some school districts with weak facilities, the insufficient video frame rate leads to a decrease in the confidence level of behaviour recognition, which in turn affects the computational stability of the hypergraph diffusion rate. Second, the model complexity is high and the deployment cost is significant. Both the fourth-order tensor convolution in STG-DM and the multi-round federation aggregation in FedCL place high demands on computational and communication resources. Although we reduce some of the overheads through Stiefel stream projection and attention compression, the real-time performance of the system may still be affected in resource-constrained environments (e.g., small and medium-sized institutions). Third, the quantification of cultural impedance factors still relies on the weighting of historical policy data, which fails to fully capture dynamic socio-cultural changes. For example, the adaptive ability of the model still lags behind in sudden policy adjustments or cross-regional cooperation. In addition, although the federal comparative learning mitigates some of the biases through knowledge distillation in the face of extreme non-independently identically distributed (non-IID) data, it still fails to fundamentally solve the problem of inconsistent model convergence. Finally, although the interpretability of the system is enhanced by heat maps and radar diagrams, there is still a ‘black box’ concern in the semantic transformation of high-dimensional spatial and temporal features to management decisions. Interpretable AI techniques (e.g., attention visualisation, feature attribution) will be introduced in the future to enhance decision transparency and user trust.

This paper proposes a cross-school educational evaluation system based on spatio-temporal graph diffusion models and federated contrastive learning. Its core contributions include: constructing an evaluation framework that balances data privacy and model performance, enabling cross-school collaboration under controllable privacy risks (ε < 1.5); Significantly enhancing predictive capability through dynamic spatio-temporal modelling, reducing prediction error by 18.7% and improving evaluation accuracy by 12.5% in heterogeneous data environments; Achieving lightweight system deployment with sub−2-second response latency, shortening decision cycles from months to near real-time. Moving forward, we shall pursue continuous optimisation across four dimensions: Enhancing cross-cultural adaptability by integrating social dynamics and meta-learning mechanisms; Deepening blockchain integration to establish traceable evaluation chains and smart contract incentive frameworks; Advancing model compression to achieve over 40% parameter reduction with no more than 3% performance degradation; Improving system interpretability by synthesising techniques such as SHAP and LIME to generate actionable management insights. These efforts will propel educational assessment towards greater security, efficiency, and transparency.
