scirep__PMC12858950.pdf.text: The inhibition of fibrosis in filtering blebs is indispensable for lowering intraocular pressure (IOP) after PRESERFLO MicroShunt surgery (PMS). We previously reported the anti-fibrotic effect of OBP-801 (OBP) on a filtering bleb in a rabbit glaucoma filtration surgery model using a 22-gauge cannula. In this study, we investigated the effect of OBP after PMS in rabbit eyes for the development of a new practically applicable anti-fibrotic treatment. This study involved 19 Japanese white rabbits that underwent PMS in the right eye, with those eyes divided into 3 groups: (1) intraoperative subconjunctival injection of 0.02% mitomycin-C (MMC) ( n = 6), (2) postoperative instillation of 100 nM OBP eye drops ( n = 7), or (3) a balanced salt solution (BSS) control ( n = 6). Bleb morphology and IOP were monitored for 12 weeks postoperative, with the bleb tissues then undergoing evaluation of fibrosis and Western blot analysis. A lower postoperative IOP was maintained in the OBP-group eyes, and at 12 weeks postoperative, the IOP was significantly lower in that group than in the BSS and MMC groups ( p < 0.01). OBP-treated eyes showed no adverse effects and reduced levels of alpha-smooth muscle actin and collagen deposition, thus suggesting that OBP is a promising candidate for improving surgical outcomes post PMS. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1038/s41598-025-34244-4. Keywords: PRESERFLO MicroShunt, OBP-801, Fibrosis, Bleb scaring, Glaucoma filtration surgery Subject terms: Drug development, Glaucoma

Glaucoma is a neurodegenerative disease characterized by the progressive dysfunction and death of retinal ganglion cells and their axons, primarily due to elevated intraocular pressure (IOP). It is the leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide, as it reportedly afflicts approximately 3.61 million people with blindness and nearly 4.14 million people with visual impairment 1 . To date, the only treatment for glaucoma is a lowering of the elevated IOP. Recently, the PRESERFLO MicroShunt (Santen Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd., Osaka, Japan), an 8.5 mm and 70 µm lumen, minimally-invasive, glaucoma drainage device that is safe and effective for not only lowering IOP, but also for reducing the number of IOP-lowering medications used, has been developed 2 – 8 . Currently, mitomycin C (MMC) is widely used during PRESERFLO MicroShunt surgery (PMS) to prevent postoperative subconjunctival fibrosis. However, it has been reported that 6.1- 44.4% of patients develop postoperative scarring in the filtration bleb that requires needling surgery 2 – 4 , 7 , suggesting that MMC does not adequately inhibit postoperative scarring in bleb tissues. In addition, there are certain risks of complications when MMC is used, such as hypotony maculopathy and leaky blebs that increase susceptibility to endophthalmitis, which subsequently leads to surgical failure 9 . It is well known that histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACi) potently target excessive fibrosis 10 , and reports have indicated that the anti-fibrotic action of HDACi will be clinically applied for the treatment of lung, kidney, and heart disease 11 , 12 . From the aspect of wound healing following tissue injury, it was previously reported that HDACi stopped corneal opacity after photorefractive keratectomy in a rabbit model 13 . OBP-801 (OBP) is a novel and potent HDACi that was identified through a p21 promoter–reporter screen 14 . Preclinical studies have demonstrated its antitumor efficacy against a wide range of solid tumors, including rhabdomyosarcoma, renal cell carcinoma, bladder cancer, ovarian cancer, neuroblastoma, and breast cancer 15 – 20 . These effects are mediated through histone hyperacetylation, cell-cycle arrest, induction of apoptosis 17 – 19 , and in some contexts, enhancement of immune responsiveness 21 . Furthermore, in a Phase Ia clinical trial involving patients with advanced solid tumors, OBP showed good tolerability, with no dose-limiting toxicities observed in the lower dose cohorts and a short plasma half-life without accumulation 22 . In addition, OBP is also a novel pluripotent epigenetic repressor of diverse genes involved in multiple steps of tissue inflammation and wound healing 23 . Moreover, OBP showed potent HDACi activity at a very low concentration, such as 1 nM; i.e., levels that are 1/1000-times lower than the standard levels thus far reported for HDACi, suberoylanilide hydroxamic acid, valproic acid (VPA) and trichostatin A 24 – 27 . In our previous investigations, we found that OBP comprehensively inhibits fibrosis, scarring, and angiogenesis in retinal pigment epithelial cells 28 . Furthermore, we previously reported that OBP eye drops inhibited postoperative scarring and maintained the filtration bleb in a rabbit glaucoma filtration surgery (GFS) model using a 22-gauge (G) cannula 23 . Thus, the aim of this present study was to investigate the effect of OBP on filtering blebs post PMS in rabbit eyes for the development of a new practically applicable antifibrotic treatment other than MMC.

scirep__PMC12858950.pdf.h2: Histone acetylation was induced by OBP in conjunctival fibroblast
scirep__PMC12858950.pdf.text: We previously reported that administering 100 nM of OBP in a rabbit GFS model effectively inhibited fibrosis 23 . To confirm the effect of HDACi on histone acetylation, we showed that OBP at a concentration of 10 nM increased acetylated histone levels in in vitro cultured human conjunctival fibroblasts (Figs. S1 , S7 ). Furthermore, we investigated whether or not histones are acetylated in in vivo conjunctival tissues, and performed western blot analysis using conjunctival tissues from naïve (non-surgical) eyes after twice-daily topical instillation of OBP (100 nM) for 1 week. Untreated conjunctival tissues from naïve eyes were used as a control. As shown in Fig. 1 , at 1 week after a twice-daily topical administration of OBP at a concentration of 100 nM, conjunctival tissues demonstrated significantly higher levels of acetylation of histone H3 (Lys9) compared to the non-treatment control ( P = 0.02).

scirep__PMC12858950.pdf.h2: OBP induced unscarred blebs with normal vascular appearance
scirep__PMC12858950.pdf.text: To examine the effect of a 100-nM OBP treatment in the morphology of the filtering bleb, we observed the filtering blebs for 12 weeks postoperative, and compared the findings among three groups: (1) eyes treated with 100 nM OBP eye drops, (2) those treated with subconjunctival injections of 0.02% MMC, and (3) those treated with balanced salt solution (BSS) (BSS Sterile Irrigating Solution; Alcon, Fort Worth, TX, USA) eye drops as a negative control (Table 1 ). Swogger et al. 29 reported that subconjunctival injections of MMC can be more effective for IOP reduction and fibrosis inhibition in the filtering bleb than the standard method of a sponge application of MMC on the bare sclera. MMC is also administered via subconjunctival injection in GFS procedures, such as used for the XEN Gel Implant (AbbVie Inc., Chicago, IL, USA) 30 . Hence, we administered MMC via subconjunctival injection in this current study based on its established use in both clinical settings and previous rabbit glaucoma model investigations. Eyes treated with BSS gradually became flat at 4-days postoperative. Conjunctival hyperemia in the superficial layers peaked at 4 days postoperative, and gradually disappeared by 2 weeks postoperative. By 4 weeks postoperative, large vessels appeared in the deeper layers of the conjunctiva, yet at 3 weeks postoperative, no major change in the appearance of bleb conjunctival tissue was observed. Finally, eyes treated with BSS were associated with a flat, yet not avascular, scarred bleb at 12 weeks postoperative (Figs. 2 and S2 ). In eyes treated with OBP, conjunctival hyperemia in the superficial layers peaked at 4 days postoperative, as in the case of the BSS group, and gradually disappeared by 1 week postoperative. Unlike the eyes that were treated with BSS, eyes treated with OBP did not show the emergence of large vessels in the deeper layers of the conjunctiva, and were found to be associated with diffuse filtering blebs of normal conjunctival appearance and without scarring at 12 weeks postoperative (Figs. 2 and S3 ). Conversely, eyes treated with MMC exhibited marked chemosis at 1 day postoperative. The conjunctival blood vessels began to disappear at 4 days postoperative, and became completely avascular at 2 weeks postoperative. The filtration blebs were associated with a thin-walled and cystic bleb with encapsulation by scar tissue at 4 weeks postoperative. After that, the filtering blebs gradually shrank via subconjunctival scarring, with the invasion of the conjunctival vessels and blebs being completely replaced with scar tissue at 12 weeks postoperative (Figs. 2 and S4 ). In addition, we quantified bleb morphology (area and vascularity) according to the scoring system developed by Fujimoto et al., which is based on the Moorfields Bleb Grading Scheme ( n = 6, 7, and 6 for BSS, OBP, and MMC, respectively) 31 , 32 . Compared with BSS, the OBP group had a significantly larger bleb area from weeks 4 through 12 ( p = 0.048, 0.008, and 0.02, respectively). In comparison with MMC, the bleb area was significantly larger in MMC at week 1 ( p = 0.01) but decreased thereafter; at week 12 the MMC bleb area was significantly smaller than that of OBP ( p = 0.004) (Fig. 2 b). For bleb vascularity, OBP remained approximately stable and did not differ significantly from BSS, whereas MMC was significantly more avascular than OBP at weeks 1 and 4 ( p = 0.001 and 0.02, respectively) and at week 12 vascularity in MMC significantly increased ( p = 0.01) (Fig. 2 c). Using a linear mixed-effects model, bleb area differed significantly between OBP and BSS across the time course ( p < 0.001), whereas no difference was detected between OBP and MMC ( p = 0.884). For bleb vascularity, the model identified a significant difference between OBP and MMC ( p = 0.007), while OBP and BSS did not differ ( p = 0.107).

scirep__PMC12858950.pdf.h2: OBP enabled IOP lowering until 12-weeks post PMS
scirep__PMC12858950.pdf.text: Since the morphology of the filtering bleb is related to postoperative IOP, we examined whether or not OBP treatment has effects that maintain the reduction of IOP after PMS. A linear mixed-effects model of the longitudinal IOP data showed significant overall differences across the time course (OBP vs. BSS, p < 0.001; OBP vs. MMC, p < 0.001). IOP in the rabbit eyes treated with BSS remained low for approximately 1-week postoperative, and then gradually increased. On the other hand, IOP in the rabbit eyes treated with OBP remained low up to 12 weeks postoperative. IOP in the rabbit eyes treated with MMC remained low for approximately 4 weeks postoperative, then gradually rose to the highest IOP among the 3 groups at 12 weeks postoperatively (Fig. 3 ). In per-time-point comparisons, IOP was maintained lower by OBP than by BSS at weeks 4, 8, and 12 ( p = 0.005, 0.049, and 0.014, respectively), and lower than by MMC at weeks 8 and 12 ( p = 0.002 and 0.001, respectively). No significant difference was found between IOP in the rabbit eyes treated with BSS and those treated with MMC at 12-weeks postoperative. As supplemental information, a post hoc power analysis of the 12-week between-group contrasts, BSS vs OBP estimated at Cohen’s d = 3.73 with power of 99.9%, and MMC vs OBP estimated at d = 4.95 with power of 99.9%.

scirep__PMC12858950.pdf.h2: OBP inhibited the expression of fibrous deposits
scirep__PMC12858950.pdf.text: Next, to investigate whether or not the differences in postoperative IOP were due to fibrosis of the filtering bleb tissue we conducted histological analysis of the tissue. At 12 weeks postoperative, hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining of the bleb tissue in the eyes treated with BSS revealed fibrous deposition in the conjunctival tissue, and immunohistochemical staining revealed the presence of a small number of α-smooth muscle antibody (α-SMA)-positive cells in the filtering blebs. The α-SMA-positive cells beneath the conjunctival epithelium coincided with conjunctival vessels, and the expression of collagen (COL) type 1 (COL-1) was observed in the subconjunctival bleb tissue, thus suggesting fibrosis in the filtering blebs (Fig. 4 a–c). On the other hand, H&E staining of the bleb tissues at 12 weeks postoperative in the eyes treated with OBP showed only mild fibrous deposition in the tissue, and immunohistochemical staining revealed that there was no existence of α-SMA-positive cells in the filtering blebs. The α-SMA-positive cells beneath the conjunctival epithelium coincided with conjunctival vessels, and sparse expression of COL-1 was observed in the bleb tissue, thus suggesting that the OBP treatment effectively suppressed fibrosis (Fig. 4 d–f). In contrast, in the eyes treated with MMC, H&E staining of the bleb tissues at 12 weeks postoperative showed the densest form of fibrous deposition in the subconjunctival tissue. Immunohistochemical staining revealed cells strongly α-SMA-positive in the bleb tissue and massive expression of COL-1, thus suggesting pronounced fibrosis in the tissue (Fig. 4 g–i). To further assess these histological findings, we quantitatively analyzed the immunofluorescence staining results measuring mean gray values of α-SMA and COL-1 signals ( n = 3, 4, and 3 for BSS, OBP, and MMC, respectively). The OBP group showed significantly lower mean gray values of COL-1 compared with the BSS group ( p = 0.010) and MMC group ( p = 0.027), and also significantly lower values of α-SMA compared with the BSS group ( p = 0.017) and MMC group ( p = 0.022). No significant differences were observed between the BSS and MMC groups for either marker (Fig. 4 j, k). Next, the bleb tissue was analyzed by western blotting at 12 weeks postoperative. The expression level of α-SMA in the MMC-group tissue was higher than that in the BSS-group tissue. Conversely, the expression of α-SMA was downregulated in the OBP-group tissue. Moreover, the expression level of COL-1 in the OBP-group tissue was lower than that in the BSS-group and MMC-group tissue, yet no statistically significant difference was observed. The expression levels of both α-SMA and COL-1 in the OBP-group tissue were extremely low, and without variation (Fig. 5 ).

scirep__PMC12858950.pdf.h2: Safety of PMS and OBP eye drops
scirep__PMC12858950.pdf.text: To investigate the safety of PMS, longitudinal slit-lamp examinations were performed. In all three groups, no leakage of aqueous humor, endophthalmitis, or cataract was observed. To elucidate if OBP eye drops caused drug toxicity, we further conducted slit-lamp examinations with fluorescein staining and terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase dUTP nick end labeling (TUNEL) assay analyses using sacrificed corneal tissue. Slit-lamp examination revealed no corneal epithelial damage, corneal opacity, or corneal edema in all rabbits. In addition, no corneal TUNEL-positive cells, which indicate apoptotic cells, were found in all groups (Fig. 6 ).

The findings in this study revealed that OBP is effective in inhibiting fibrosis of the bleb tissue and maintaining lower IOP for 3 months post PMS in rabbit eyes. Although various agents have been reported to be effective in inhibiting postoperative fibrosis following GFS in a rabbit model 33 – 38 , our findings demonstrate for the first time that OBP can be a new, practically-applicable antifibrotic treatment to maintain decreased IOP and inhibit bleb scarring, thus making it an excellent alternative to MMC post PMS. In the clinical setting, MMC is topically applied, followed by washing with saline, to inhibit postoperative fibrosis of the filtration bleb in PMS 2 – 4 , 7 . In addition, in cases of GFS, 5-FU is sometimes administered via subconjunctival injection to inhibit postoperative fibrosis 39 . We previously reported that when OBP is topically administered as eye drops, it is as effective as subconjunctival injections for preventing postoperative fibrosis 23 . In this current study, our findings confirmed that acetylation of histone H3 was significantly increased in the conjunctival tissue at 1-week post topical administration. Furthermore, administering OBP as eye drops also effectively prevented fibrosis of the filtration bleb for 3 months after PMS. OBP is effective even when administered via eye drops, thus providing practical advantages over MMC, which is limited to intraoperative application only. This makes it possible to easily add OBP post surgery. Therefore, in cases where there are strong postoperative fibrosis and a high risk of scarring at the filtration bleb, OBP can be used for a longer period. Moreover, if fibrosis reoccurs, the treatment can easily be resumed due to its administration as eye drops, allowing for a flexible application tailored to individual cases. 5-FU is usually administered after surgery via a subconjunctival injection, which is more invasive. While MMC has antifibrotic effects, formation of avascular areas and thinning of the walls of the filtration bleb can also occur, which ultimately leads to leakage of aqueous humor from the bleb and an increase in the risk of infection post GFS. Fujimoto et al. 32 also reported the formation of avascular areas following PMS with MMC in rabbit eyes, which is consistent with the results in this study. Although no postoperative infections were observed in either study, the risk remains. In contrast, the filtration blebs in the OBP-treated group in this study were flat, not avascular, and non-scarred, thus more closely resembling normal conjunctiva. In addition, our findings demonstrated that there were no corneal epithelial defects or toxicity to the corneal stroma in the OBP group, and indicate that OBP contributes to a lower risk of postoperative infection and lessens the risk of scarring, thus displaying its potential for safe use. In regard to systemic safety, it has been generally reported that topical ophthalmic medications rarely result in clinically meaningful systemic accumulation because they are designed to minimize systemic absorption, with some variability depending on the drug 40 . As OBP was administered in this study via topical eye drops at a nanomolar concentration (i.e., 100 nM), we believe that even if one drop was absorbed systemically, the plasma levels would remain below the detectable limit. Furthermore, the findings in a Phase Ia clinical trial of OBP in patients with advanced solid tumors demonstrated that no dose-limiting toxicities were observed in the low-dose cohort (i.e., 1.0 mg/m 2 ), and that OBP exhibited a very short plasma half-life (i.e., 0.2–0.7 h) without accumulation, thus supporting the plausibility of its safe use as an ophthalmic formulation 22 . The PM is composed of styrene-b-isobutylene-b-styrene, a highly biocompatible material, and reportedly reduces the likelihood of conjunctival scarring in rabbit eyes 41 . However, it was reported that PMS without antifibrotic treatment resulted in the deposition of thick, disorganized collagen fibers in the filtering bleb by 28 days after surgery 27 . In this present study, immunohistochemical staining of the filtration bleb tissues at 12-weeks postoperative similarly detected higher levels of COL-1 expression and α-SMA-positive cells in the BSS group compared to the OBP group, with western blot analysis confirming an increase in those proteins, consequently leading to a gradual increase in IOP in the BSS group. These findings suggest the necessity of using antifibrotic agents when performing PMS. Fujimoto et al. 32 reported that even when MMC is used in conjunction with PMS on rabbit eyes, immunohistochemical staining of the filtration bleb from 2- to 12 weeks postoperative showed deposition of α-SMA and COL-1, which is consistent with our findings that the MMC group exhibited more deposition of α-SMA and COL-1 compared to the OBP group, and western blot analysis also showed substantial expression of these proteins. The remodeling caused by excessive fibrosis may have induced the recurrence of elevated IOP post surgery, as evidenced by our findings where the MMC group exhibited a rise in IOP in the later postoperative period. It was recently reported that the combined therapy of 0.03% VPA and low-dose MMC (0.1 mg/mL) is more effective than high-dose MMC (0.4 mg/mL) in inhibiting fibrosis of the filtering bleb at 28 days after PMS 26 , 27 . Like OBP, 0.03% VPA is an HDACi that suppresses fibrosis, however, the results in those previous studies were short-term (i.e., 28 days postoperative), and the authors did not clearly elucidate the reduction of IOP post surgery, which is a very important outcome. Moreover, VPA must be administered via subconjunctival injection at every postoperative follow-up. OBP, on the other hand, can be administered via eye drops at a much lower concentration of 100 nM, and it not only suppresses fibrosis but also maintains IOP reduction for 3-months postoperative, thus demonstrating its potential as an effective and less invasive antifibrotic agent for PMS. In our findings, while preoperative subconjunctival injection of MMC led to an increase in IOP at 12-weeks post PMS, the pre- and postoperative topical administration of OBP contributed to maintaining IOP reduction in the rabbit-model eyes, similar to the results in our previous report involving a rabbit GFS model 23 . In another previous report involving rabbit eyes, the findings indicated that at 12 weeks after surgery, PMS combined with 0.04% MMC maintained IOP reduction comparable to the level in the GFS model 32 . In that study, MMC was applied and then washed off with saline, thus possibly weakening the assessment of its efficacy compared to a subconjunctival injection of 0.02% MMC. In the clinical setting, there are sometimes cases in which IOP increases due to scarring of the filtration bleb even with the application of MMC post GFS, and we posit that the MMC group in this current study may have replicated such cases.

It should be noted that this study had several limitations. First, the sample size in this exploratory preclinical study was small. For the IOP endpoint, a post hoc power analysis of the 12-week intergroup comparisons indicated high power at the observed effect sizes. However, post hoc power analysis depends on the observed effect sizes. With a small sample size, the precision of effect estimates decreases, so the results should be interpreted with caution. Second, steroids were not used, even though they commonly are used after PMS. Postoperative glucocorticoids are understood to act primarily upstream by suppressing the inflammatory cascade including cytokine release and leukocyte infiltration, thereby contributing to the reduction of postoperative fibrosis and scarring 42 . At present, and to the best of our knowledge, there have been no studies evaluating the effects of OBP in the presence of postoperative glucocorticoids. However, in our previous report we modeled an inflamed postoperative environment in vitro using transforming growth factor beta (TGF-β) 2 with or without tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α) and found that OBP (i.e., 0.5–1 nM) almost completely prevented TGF-β–driven myofibroblast transition in human primary conjunctival fibroblasts, suppressing α-SMA and COL-I, -III, and -XVI 23 . In that study, OBP also reduced induction of the lysyl oxidase (LOX)/LOX-like (LOXL) family - key extracellular matrix cross-linking enzymes - indicating restraint of both matrix production and matrix maturation even under pro-inflammatory stimulation, and our findings demonstrated in vivo downregulation of TGF-β3, COL1A, and LOX, and reduced α-SMA and COL-1 proteins in bleb tissue. Since these mechanisms are likely complementary, we speculate that combining OBP with conventional postoperative steroid therapy may provide additive or even synergistic antifibrotic effects, which should be evaluated in future studies. Third, systemic safety was not comprehensively assessed. Although previous clinical data suggest favorable tolerability and topical ophthalmic dosing typically yields minimal systemic exposure, this current study did not include formal systemic toxicology. We observed no local ocular toxicity or serious systemic adverse events, such as sudden death; however, further systemic organ assessments and exposure profiling are warranted to support future clinical development of OBP as an ophthalmic formulation. Fourth, corneal fluorescence and TUNEL staining were only evaluated at 12-weeks postoperative, i.e., when tissue responses were expected to be stable. Early postoperative changes were not assessed, as they may largely reflect surgical invasion and acute inflammation rather than the direct effects of the administered agents, which could complicate the interpretation of drug-related toxicity. Further studies are needed to confirm both local and systemic safety following topical ocular administration.

The findings in this study revealed that OBP, a pluripotent epigenetic regulator, attenuates fibrosis of the filtering bleb and maintains IOP reduction for 12 weeks post PMS in rabbit eyes, and suggest that a PMS and OBP combined treatment could be an ideal GFS to maintain IOP reduction with a healthy wound-healing process. For clinical application, the long-term effect of the combination of OBP and steroid requires further investigation.

Adult female Japanese white rabbits (2.5–3.0 kg in weight) were obtained from Shimizu Laboratory Supplies (Kyoto, Japan) and used for the PMS rabbit-model experiments performed in this study. PM devices were provided by Santen Pharmaceutical. For adaptation to the laboratory environment, all rabbits were kept in separate cages in the laboratory for 1 week prior to undergoing PMS. On the day of the operation, PMS was performed on the right eye of each rabbit under general anesthesia with intramuscular injections of a mixture of 50 mg/kg ketamine hydrochloride (Daiichi Sankyo Propharma Co., Ltd., Tokyo, Japan) and 10 mg/kg xylazine hydrochloride (Bayer Yakuhin, Ltd., Osaka, Japan), combined with a topical administration of oxybuprocaine eye drops (Santen Pharmaceutical). PMS was performed as follows. First, a fornix-base conjunctival incision was made in the upper quadrant, either superior-temporally or superior-nasally. Approximately 3 mm from the limbus, a scleral pocket of about 1.2 mm was created using a MVR Lance 20G (MANI, Inc., Utsunomiya, Japan). From within that scleral pocket, a pathway for device insertion was created toward the anterior chamber angle using a 25 G needle (Nipro Corporation, Settsu, Japan) through which a PM was then inserted. Properly inserted, the PM protruded 2 or 3 mm into the anterior chamber without contacting the iris or cornea, with its fins positioned to fit within the scleral pocket. Finally, the Tenon’s capsule and conjunctiva were sutured with 10–0 nylon (MANI) (Fig. 7 a, b). At the end of surgery, 1 drop of 1% atropine sulfate (Nitten Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd., Nagoya, Japan) and an ointment of 0.1% betamethasone sodium phosphate and 0.35% fradiomycin sulfate (Shionogi & Co., Ltd., Osaka, Japan) was applied. Each surgery was performed by a single experienced surgeon (T.I). All evaluation of subjective/qualitative grading measures, such as bleb appearance and the histology of the rabbits that underwent PMS, were carried out by persons other than the surgeon who performed the operations in a masked fashion.

A 250 μM (20 mg/ 20 ml) stock solution and 10 μM sub-stock solution of OBP was prepared by dissolving it in dimethyl sulfoxide, and it was subsequently stored at -30 °C. OBP was then dissolved at 100 nM in BSS . According to our previous reports, OBP at a concentration 10 or 100 times higher than that resulting in the in vitro suppression of α-SMA and COL-1 was administered. The stock MMC solution (Kyowa Hakko Kirin Co., Ltd., Tokyo, Japan) was dissolved in BSS at 0.2%, and then diluted to 0.02% at the time of use. BSS and OBP were administered as eye drops, and MMC was administered via subconjunctival injection in a well-tolerated applied regimen without serious adverse events. Rabbits undergoing PMS were classified into the following 3 treatment groups: (1) BSS group ( n = 6 rabbits that received 4 eye drops of 20 μL of BSS at 30 min before surgery and twice daily for 7 days postoperative); (2) OBP group ( n = 7 rabbits that received 4 eye drops of 20 μL of 100 nM OBP solution at 30 s intervals at 30 min before surgery and twice daily for 7 days postoperative); (3) MMC group ( n = 6 rabbits that received a 100 μL subconjunctival injection of 0.02% MMC solution at 30 min before surgery).

scirep__PMC12858950.pdf.h2: Clinical evaluation of the effects in the PMS rabbit-model
scirep__PMC12858950.pdf.text: To assess the safety and efficacy, the anterior segment of the eyes, bleb appearance, and IOP were evaluated prior to PMS and at 1-day and 1-, 4-, 8-, and 12 weeks postoperative. We quantified bleb morphology according to the scoring system developed by Fujimoto et al., which is based on the Moorfields Bleb Grading Scheme and was applied to the rabbit PMS model 31 , 32 . In specific, the bleb area was graded on a 5-point ordinal scale (i.e., 0 = no bleb, 1 = very small bleb, 2 = small bleb, 3 = medium bleb, and 4 = large bleb) and vascularity was graded on a 4-point ordinal scale (i.e., 1 = avascular, 2 = normal vascularity, 3 = mild vessel inflammation, and 4 = moderate or severe inflammation). The scores were obtained longitudinally at 1-day and 1-, 4-, 8-, and 12 weeks postoperative, and were independently evaluated by two ophthalmologists using blinded bleb-photograph data ( n = 6, 7, and 6 for BSS, OBP, and MMC, respectively). IOP was measured in both eyes (3 times per eye) of each rabbit with a tonometer (iCare TONOVET; iCare Finland Oy, Vantaa, Finland), with the median value of the 3 measurements then calculated 43 .

At 12 weeks after PMS, each rabbit was euthanized with an overdose of pentobarbital sodium (100 mg/kg), administered intravenously through the marginal ear vein using a sterile syringe and a 27-gauge needle. Both eyes were enucleated, and the bleb tissues were sectioned. Conjunctival tissue obtained from the non-operated contralateral eye of each rabbit was used as a control. The tissues were stained with H&E stain. Immunofluorescence staining for α-SMA, a marker of myofibroblasts, using mouse anti-α-SMA antibody (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA), and COL-1 using mouse anti-COL-1 antibody (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA), was performed. Images were obtained using a dual-sensor, charge-coupled device (CCD), microscope digital camera (DP80; Olympus Corporation, Tokyo, Japan) for the H&E staining and a confocal laser-scanning microscope (FV-1200; Olympus Corporation) for the immunofluorescence staining. Immunofluorescence images were imported into FIJI (ImageJ, version 1.54f., National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD, USA). The staining signals of α-SMA and COL-1 were selected using the polygon selection tool, and the images were converted to 8-bit grayscale. Mean gray values were measured, and the averages ± standard deviation (SD) were calculated from representative images for each group ( n = 3, 4, and 3 for BSS, OBP, and MMC, respectively).

For the analysis of bleb tissues, each rabbit was sacrificed at 12-weeks postoperative and treated with the above-described procedures. The isolated bleb tissue was put into a 1.5-mL tube and frozen in liquid nitrogen. The frozen tissue was cut into small pieces (5 mm × 5 mm in size), and lysed with radioimmunoprecipitation assay buffer containing a protease/phosphatase inhibitor cocktail (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The tissue was then thoroughly ground with Fisherbrand™ Pellet Pestles™ (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and sonicated at 30s intervals for 5 min and rotatory mixed for several hours. Next, the supernatant was collected by centrifugation at 10,000 × g for 20 min at 4 °C, and the protein concentration was measured using the Pierce™ BCA Protein Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The blocking and detection reaction were performed using the iBind Western System (Thermo Fisher Scientific) after sodium dodecyl sulfate–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis on 4–12% gel. The primary antibodies, mouse anti-histone H3 (1:1000) (MAB Institute, Nagano, Japan), mouse anti-acetyl histone H3 (Lys8) (1:200) (MAB Institute), mouse anti-α-SMA (1:500) (Sigma-Aldrich), mouse anti-COL-1 (1:500, Thermo Fisher Scientific), and mouse anti-GAPDH (1:2000) (Medical & Biological Laboratories Co., Inc., Tokyo, Japan) antibodies were used, and goat anti-mouse IgG HRP conjugate (1:1000) (Southern Biotech, Birmingham, AL, USA) antibody was used as a secondary antibody. The protein bands were made visible with the Western BLoT chemiluminescent substrate series; Quant, Hyper, or Ultra Sensitive HRP Substrate (TaKaRa Bio Inc., Shiga, Japan). Luminescence was observed using ImageQuant LAS-3000 (FUJIFILM, Tokyo, Japan), a CCD camera system. Semi-quantification of the density of each band was conducted using the Image J software program (1.54i; National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD, USA) with GAPDH as the reference protein.

Descriptive statistics are expressed as mean ± SD of the mean of at least 3 independent experiments. Relative intensity of Western blot analysis and the mean gray value of immunofluorescence images were analyzed by the t -test. Longitudinal changes in IOP, bleb area and vascularity were analyzed using a linear mixed-effects model with treatment (OBP, BSS, MMC) and time as fixed effects and rabbit as a random intercept. Time points were baseline, 1 day, 1, 4, 8, and 12 weeks for IOP, and 1 day, 1, 4, 8, and 12 weeks for bleb area and vascularity. For between-group comparison at each time point, we used Dunn’s multiple comparisons test. This was an exploratory preclinical study. Therefore, a priori sample-size calculations were not performed because effect sizes and variance estimates were unavailable at the design stage. For the IOP endpoint at 12-weeks postoperative, we conducted a post hoc power analysis for three pairwise comparisons (i.e., OBP vs. BSS, OBP vs. MMC, and BSS vs. MMC), estimating power from the observed mean differences, SDs, and group sizes. To account for the three comparisons, we applied a Bonferroni-adjusted correction: α = 0.0167. The statistical analyses were conducted using the R software environment (The R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria), and a p value of < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

scirep__PMC12859102.pdf.text: Drying is a widely employed preservation method in food processing, aimed at extending shelf life by reducing moisture content, thereby minimizing storage and transportation costs. Despite their widespread use, cabinet-type multi-tray dryers often exhibit non-uniform airflow distribution, leading to inconsistent airflow uniformity. This study presents an optimization framework to enhance airflow uniformity by strategically repositioning supply fans, integrating Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations with Sequential Linear Programming (SLP). An L 25 orthogonal array guided the CFD experiment design, and a second-order polynomial regression model was developed to correlate the airflow uniformity index (U i ) with fan positions (P 1 , P 2 , P 3 ). The optimization, constrained by fixed geometric and operational parameters including a 78.80 mm supply gap, 45° baffle angle, 2.74 m/s Inlet airflow speed and 315 mm fan diameter was conducted for a 32-tray dryer (dimensions: 1420 × 650 × 1600 mm). The regression model achieved R² = 0.9247. Incorporating trust-region techniques into the SLP framework significantly improved convergence efficiency: static and dynamic trust-region approaches reduced iterations to 15 and 8, respectively, compared to 661 without trust-region control. These methods adaptively managed step sizes, promoting faster and more stable convergence without compromising accuracy. The MATLAB-based optimization yielded optimal fan positions of P 1 = 359.05 mm, P 2 = 395 mm, and P 3 = 395 mm, achieving a maximum uniformity of 76.5% with 0.2% prediction error. This CFD–SLP integrated approach offers a reliable, scalable, and cost-effective solution for enhancing airflow uniformity in industrial dryers and holds promise for broader applications such as thermal or fluid process optimization tasks across food, pharmaceutical, and chemical industries. Keywords: Multi-tray cabinet dryer, Airflow uniformity, Computational fluid dynamics, Sequential linear programming, Trust-region methods, Fan positioning optimization Subject terms: Energy science and technology, Engineering, Materials science, Mathematics and computing

There is an increasing trend in the global food market industries to improve the food products value chains through different techniques 1 . Drying is one of the most common food preservation techniques 2 . Drying can minimize the storage and transportation costs, and makes handling easier by reducing size and weight. It is the process of moisture removal due to the simultaneous heat and mass transfer under controlled conditions. Efforts have been made recently to develop dried foods with high quality by using innovative technologies. The drying technologies can reduce the water activity to a level with no microbiological activity and biochemical reactions. Most commonly, the efficiency of a dryer is dependent on air flow speed and drying air temperature 3 , 4 . Based on a most recent comprehensive review 5 , Increasing the drying temperature and airflow speed significantly accelerates moisture evaporation and reduces drying time, via enhancing both heat and mass transfer. Advancement on sun drying leads to solar drying. The artificial method of drying technologies such as cabinet, tunnel, conveyor, fluidized bed, drum and vacuum shelf. During drying, water from the surface evaporates by mass and heat transfer mechanisms resulting in a reduction of the water activity of the product 5 – 9 . In a cabinet type multi tray dryer, more products can be loaded as the trays are arranged at different levels 10 . The key to a quality operation of those dryers is uniformity of hot airflow distribution over trays. However, multi-tray dryers (large size industrial dryers), encounter poor airflow speed uniformity. This study focused on optimizing the positions of the supply fans to enhance airflow distribution, while other design elements such as airflow-guiding baffles and the supply zone gap beneath the wire mesh trays were kept fixed 5 , 11 . This research specifically focused on optimizing the position of the supply fans under a fixed supply zone gap (78.80 mm) and baffle angles (45°, downward) 12 – 14 . As illustrated in Fig. 2 , three supply fans were positioned centrally on each side along the height of the dryer. A fan with a diameter of ∅315 mm and six impellers, each set at a 10° impeller angle (AXC 315-6/12°-4-PV axial fan, https://www.systemair.com ), was selected based on the calculated static pressure and volume flow rate requirement (15.56 pa and 0.252 m³/s). The size and capacity of the fans and the drying unit are presented in Table 1 . CFD has been utilized in different types of food drying applications, to substitute expensive experimental trials and predict distribution of airflow speed and temperature uniformity in the drying chamber 15 – 17 . CFD simulation to obtain a uniform distribution of drying air flow speed and temperature by changing the angle of baffles and position of exhaust, with three trays under electric resistance heat source shows purely uniform distribution of temperature. However, the airflow distribution ranges from 0.016 m/s to 3.89 m/s over the entire drying unit 15 . The most resent design and simulation of airflow speed on multi tray dryer to improve uniformity by using CFD with 18 trays shows a range of distribution of airflow speed from 0 m/s to 6 m/s over the drying unit with 6.17 m/s inlet airflow speed 18 . The same wise research on prediction of drying uniformity of multi tray dryer with 21 trays, were assumed as porous media with 10% porosity has simulated on CFD. Results show better uniformity of distribution of heat on 18 trays. However, the airflow speed over the drying unit varies from 0 m/s to 3 m/s with 3 m/s inlet airflow speed 10 . Sequential Linear Programming (SLP), also known as Successive Linear Programming, is an iterative method used to solve nonlinear constrained optimization problems by converting them into a sequence of linear programming problems 19 . This approach is based on successive first-order linearizations of the objective and constraint functions. SLP has been successfully applied to optimize complex nonlinear problems in various fields, including heat distribution in living spaces 20 , optimal selection of auxiliary fans 21 , hybrid renewable energy systems 22 , and pick-and-place task optimization 23 , resulting in significant airflow uniformity improvements. The study aims to strategically reposition the dryer’s supply fans to achieve more consistent airflow and enhance airflow uniformity, using CFD simulation and SLP optimization techniques. Specifically, the research focuses on: Developing a CFD-based fluid model of the dryer and perform mesh-independence tests for reliable airflow predictions. Generating surface plots and fitting regression models linking airflow uniformity index (U i ) to fan position parameters using DOE data. Applying SLP for optimizing fan positions and to enhance convergence using static and dynamic trust-region strategies. Validating the optimized solutions by comparing SLP-predicted U i values with CFD-simulated results and quantifying accuracy using percentage error. A second-order polynomial model, representing fan positional configurations, was derived from Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) results obtained via experiments based on an L 25 orthogonal array design. The model’s behavior was analysed using nonlinear surface plots and curve fitting. Optimization of the fan positions then followed, employing SLP with static and dynamic trust-region strategies, further guided by insights from literatures on drying chamber design modifications 7 , 11 , 15 , 24 .

This study employed a structured methodology to optimize multi-tray dryer performance. The workflow (Fig. 1 ) outlines the process, integrating experimental design, CFD modeling with mesh verification, polynomial surface fitting, sequential linear programming-based optimization, and validation of the optimized configuration.

After identifying the controlled and fixed factors (summarized in Table 4 ), an L 25 (5³) orthogonal array experimental design was implemented using Minitab statistical software. The factors P 1 , P 2 , and P 3 , corresponding to the gap between supply fans, were varied at five levels each (207, 254, 301, 348, and 395 mm), as illustrated in Fig. 2 a. The airflow speed uniformity index (U i ) was selected as the dependent variable to evaluate airflow uniformity. Details of the controlled and fixed factors are provided in Table 2 . For each DOE run, simulations were performed using ANSYS 2022 R1, ANSYS Fluent, and the airflow speed uniformity was quantified using the area-weighted uniformity index.

scirep__PMC12859102.pdf.h2: Fluid modelling and mesh dependency test
scirep__PMC12859102.pdf.text: For each experiment design a fluid model was created by subtracting the solid structures of the dryer, such as the body, baffles, wire mesh trays, and trolley from a 2D model (Fig. 2 b). The resulting geometry was saved in .igs format and imported into Design Modeler in ANSYS Fluent for each simulation run. Figure 3 a illustrates the 3D fluid model of the dryer. As shown on Table 3 a mesh dependency analysis was conducted by varying mesh sizes while keeping all boundary conditions constant. Three mesh sizes 0.0125 m, 0.01 m, and 0.0075 m were tested, and airflow speed convergence was evaluated at a fixed point (L, W, H) = (1.2, 0.3, 0.6 m) on tray 8. The variation in predicted airflow speed between the two finest meshes was only 0.41%, confirming mesh independence. Consequently, the medium mesh (0.010 m, approximately 7.8 million elements) was selected as the optimal configuration, offering a balance between computational cost and solution accuracy. Figure 3 (b) shows the symmetry of dryer meshed with 0.01 m, with a zoom in sectional view. ANSYS Fluent reported a high overall mesh quality of 0.999, while global mesh skewness metrics indicated good numerical quality, with a maximum of 0.17, average of 0.08, and minimum of 0.04, all well within the acceptable range (< 0.95), ensuring accurate and stable numerical performance. In addition, mesh adaptation was applied during the simulation to maintain mesh independence and further enhance accuracy 10 . Convergence of the flow solution was verified through the residual histories shown in Fig. 4 . The residuals for momentum, turbulence kinetic energy (k), and specific dissipation rate (ω) decreased below 10⁻⁴, while the continuity residual dropped by more than two orders of magnitude. These results confirm that the final solution achieved both numerical stability and physical consistency within the first 150 iterations. Based on this, all runs were conducted with a maximum of 150 iterations.

scirep__PMC12859102.pdf.h2: Model selection and boundary conditions setup
scirep__PMC12859102.pdf.text: The inlet airflow speed was set to 2.74 m/s based on prior research, with a turbulence intensity of 5% and a turbulence length scale of 0.07 × the inlet diameter (315 mm). The outlet was specified as a pressure outlet at 0 MPa (gauge). All walls were assumed smooth, with negligible roughness effects. Baffles were represented as solid internal surfaces, with angles fixed according to previous studies. Since this study focuses on airflow rather than heat distribution, the energy equations were not considered. Air was treated as an incompressible working fluid with default thermophysical properties in ANSYS Fluent. Buoyancy effects were neglected because the flow was dominated by forced convection, and the maximum velocity corresponded to a Mach number far below 0.3. To achieve accurate airflow predictions, selecting an appropriate turbulence model is essential. As this study does not focus on heat distribution, the energy equations were not considered. The standard k-ε model performs well for turbulent shear flows but is less accurate for flows with adverse pressure gradients, rotation, or streamline curvature. In the drying process, the presence of baffles (air diffusers), heating coils, and wire mesh trays generates strain flows and static pressure differences, where the k-ε model may not predict airflow circulation accurately. The k-ω model is more effective for boundary layers with adverse pressure gradients and separated flows, and it can also handle turbulent flows in porous media 10 , 25 . An improved version, the SST k-ω model, combines the advantages of k-ε and k-ω models across the domain. Therefore, the SST k-ω model was selected to accurately predict airflow over the walls and wire mesh trays.

Based on the U i results corresponding to each DOE point, surface plots of U i versus P 1 , P 2 and P 3 were generated with origin 2018 software to gain insight into the input-output relationships. A 4D surface plot was constructed. Subsequently, polynomial nonlinear surface fitting was performed, and a second-order polynomial regression model with interaction terms for P 1 , P 2 and P 3 was developed using the analysis of variance (ANOVA) technique.

scirep__PMC12859102.pdf.h2: Sequential linear programming-based optimization and validation
scirep__PMC12859102.pdf.text: This study employs a Sequential Linear Programming (SLP) in MATLAB R2024b to optimize the positions of supply fans in a multi-tray cabinet dryer, with the objective of maximizing the airflow uniformity index (U i ). The optimization framework was implemented in MATLAB, beginning with an initial guess for the design variables (P 1 , P 2 , P 3 ). The design variables were iteratively updated based on a small step size (α = 0.01), which ensured stability and reduced the risk of overshooting the optimum solution. Convergence was determined when the norm of the design variable update between successive iterations fell below a tolerance threshold (tol = 1e − 6 ), with a maximum of 1000 iterations allowed to facilitate sufficient exploration of the design space. In addition to this baseline SLP configuration, an enhanced SLP framework incorporating trust-region strategies was established to further regulate the step size and directionality of the search process. This method constrains the updates within a trust region defined by a radius vector Δ, ensuring that steps remain within a bounded local neighbourhood. The optimization incorporated an exponentially decaying step size mechanism, where the step size α was reduced over iterations according to a decay rate (α₀ = 1, decay rate = 0.95), with a lower bound (α min = 0.01) to prevent stagnation. This adaptive strategy enables large, exploratory steps during the early iterations and progressively finer updates as convergence nears, facilitating both rapid progress and precise refinement. Two distinct trust-region schemes were implemented to guide the optimization process. In the Static Trust Region approach, the trust region radius decays progressively over iterations. A step is accepted if the improvement ratio (ρ) defined as the ratio of actual to predicted improvement is positive (ρ > 0). If the step is rejected (ρ ≤ 0), the trust region radius is reduced by 5%, with a lower bound set at 0.01 to maintain sufficient search flexibility. In contrast, the Dynamic Trust Region method adaptively adjusts the radius based on model prediction accuracy. When ρ > 0.75, indicating a high degree of agreement between predicted and actual improvements, the trust region is expanded to allow broader exploration. Conversely, if ρ < 0.25, suggesting poor model fidelity, the region is contracted to enforce more conservative steps. This adaptive mechanism allows the optimizer to respond to the local landscape of the objective function, promoting stability and ensuring tighter convergence near the optimum. Importantly, the decaying step size and trust region mechanisms operate independently, with the former enforcing global control over the step magnitude, and the latter enforcing local directional constraints. At each iteration, the nonlinear objective function (U i ) is locally approximated using a linear model. The gradient of the objective function is computed using central finite differences, and the resulting linear programming subproblem is solved using MATLAB’s linprog function. The solver minimizes the negative gradient while respecting the bounds on the design variables and the trust region constraints. Finally, to evaluate the fidelity of the SLP model, predicted U i values were compared against the actual values computed via CFD simulations at the optimal fan positions by using the percentage error metric defined in Eq. (1). Additionally, a parity plot comparing the predicted and CFD-obtained airflow speed uniformity index (U i ) confirms the reliability and practical applicability of the proposed SLP-based optimization framework for enhancing airflow uniformity in drying systems.

Based on the CFD results, the positions of the supply fans at 25 design points designated as P 1 , P 2 , P 3 were evaluated for their effect on the airflow speed uniformity index (U i ). The corresponding values of P 1 , P 2 , P 3 , and U i are presented in Table 4 . As shown in Fig. 5 b, 4D surface plotting was performed using the design of experiments (DOE) data before fitting the model to visually analyse the relationship between the input parameters (P 1 , P 2 , P 3 ) and the response variable (U i ). This visualization provided insight into how changes in factor levels influence the output nonlinearly, supporting the selection of a suitable regression model. As shown in Fig. 5 a, each coloured surface illustrates how the uniformity index (U i ) varies with P 2 and P 3 while holding P 1 constant at one of five selected design values. Comparing these surfaces reveals that the overall landscape of U i ​ shifts upward as P 1 ​ increases, with the lowest values occurring around P 1 = 207 mm, and peak uniformity emerging near P 1 = 348 mm. Based on the data presented in Table 4 and the surface plot in Fig. 5 (b), a second-order polynomial regression model with interaction terms for P 1 , P 2 , and P 3 was developed. The resulting fitted surface, shown alongside the actual data points (Fig. 6 ), illustrates the accuracy of the model in capturing the variation in the uniformity index (U i ). The mathematical expression of this relationship is provided in Eq. (2). The model achieved a coefficient of determination R² of 0.9247, indicating that approximately 92.47% of the variability with a high level of predictive reliability (95%). Figure 6 b shows the comparison between predicted and actual values of the airflow speed uniformity index (U i ). The scatter plot demonstrates how closely the model’s predictions align with the observed CFD results. The red dashed line representing an ideal fit (Predicted U i =Actual U i ), where perfect prediction would lie. The points cluster closely around this line, indicating good model accuracy and consistency, further supported by a high R² value (0.9247) and RMSE of 0.0037. The corresponding data used for this plot is presented in Table 4 .

Sequential linear programming was employed to determine the optimum positions of the supply fans, considering the airflow uniformity index (U i ) as the objective function and P 1 , P 2 and P 3 as design constraints. As a result of using SLP with and without trust region strategies, the optimal positions of the supply fans in the multi-tray cabinet dryer were successfully identified. By considering a strict convergence tolerance (tol = 1e − 6 ), the nonlinear objective function (U i ) was efficiently maximized. Compared to the SLP method without trust region, which required approximately 650 iterations to converge (Fig. 7 c), SLP with static trust region approach together with adaptive step size (decreasing in every iteration) decayed the region size at each iteration and prevents getting stuck in small updates, Fig. 7 e. While, the dynamic approach has adaptively expanded or contracted the trust region based on the step acceptance criteria. As illustrated in Fig. 7 g, This approach ensured convergence in fewer iterations and provided a straightforward design path. Both trust-region methods demonstrated substantially faster convergence compared to the standard SLP approach without trust-region control, which required approximately 661 iterations to converge (Fig. 7 c), following a complex zigzagging path (Fig. 7 d). In contrast, the trust-region strategies facilitated a more stable and directed optimization process with minimal iterations. A steady increase in the U i value was observed, characterized by rapid improvements during early iterations and gradual stabilization as the algorithm approached the optimum. This behavior is attributed to the use of a small step size, which played a crucial role in regulating search direction, minimizing the risk of overshooting, and preventing oscillations around local optima. The carefully chosen parameters ensured an effective balance between convergence speed and solution quality, enabling the algorithm to closely approximate the global maximum. Among trust region-based methods, the lowest prediction error (0.201%) was achieved, indicating high accuracy of the optimization outcome within the defined design bounds. In contrast, the SLP with a static trust region converged in just 15 iterations (Fig. 7 e), and the dynamic trust region approach achieved convergence in only 8 iterations (Fig. 7 g). As revealed on Table 5 , these trust region strategies did not significantly alter the optimal solution values. As shown in Fig. 7 g and h, the dynamic trust region method provided the fastest convergence and the smoothest optimization path, exhibiting minimal zigzagging behavior compared to the static trust region strategy (Fig. 7 f). Overall, incorporating a trust region particularly a dynamic one substantially improved convergence speed and efficiency, as shown in Table 5 . The SLP algorithm with dynamic trust region ultimately converged to an optimal configuration with fan positions of P 1 = 359.0482 mm, P 2 = 395 mm, and P 3 = 395 mm, achieving a maximum U i value of 0.76604. This result demonstrates both the stability and effectiveness of SLP in navigating and optimizing within a nonlinear design space. When compared to recent studies 26 – 28 , a significant improvement in airflow uniformity has achieved. Further insights were gained through 3D surface and contour plots (Fig. 7 a and b) respectively, through fixing P 3 at its optimal value and varying P 1 and P 2 . These plots clearly depict a smooth, unimodal response surface, with the U i value increasing toward a peak in the region around the optimized coordinates. The smooth curvature and absence of abrupt changes suggest that the linear approximations used in SLP are valid within the local neighbour hoods explored at each iteration. This confirms the effectiveness of SLP in handling moderately nonlinear systems and highlights its suitability for real-world engineering optimization problems, where computational efficiency and interpretability are important.

To validate the model’s predictive capability beyond the optimized region, additional DOE points were evaluated by randomly selecting P 1 , P 2 , and P 3 within the range of 207–395 mm. Figure 8 presents a parity plot comparing the predicted and CFD-obtained airflow speed uniformity index (U i ), at 95% confidence intervals. The scatter points closely follow the red dashed line representing the ideal fit, indicating strong agreement between the surrogate model and CFD results. This confirms good generalization performance, with R² = 0.9315 and RMSE = 0.0021. Although the original objective function (U i ) is nonlinear and derived from CFD-based approximations, the Sequential Linear Programming (SLP) method, which employs linear approximations using gradient information at each iteration successfully approximated the optimal solution. As shown in Fig. 8 , the parity plot demonstrates close agreement between the predicted and actual U i values, while Table 5 indicates a very small prediction error. The SLP optimization achieved near-optimal supply fan positions (P 1 , P 2 , and P 3 ) without overshooting or instability. Notably, the SLP approach without trust-region strategies yielded a minimum error of 0.201%. and required 1.069 s of CPU time. Introducing a static trust region reduced the error to 0.356% with a CPU time of 0.0858 s, while the dynamic trust region approach achieved an error of 0.241% in only 0.0757 s. These results demonstrate that trust-region strategies, particularly dynamic adjustment, not only maintain accuracy but also substantially reduce computational cost. The consistently low errors across all approaches further confirm the reliability of the regression-based U i function employed in the optimization process. As shown in Fig. 9 (a), high-velocity regions remain concentrated near the outlet walls, while the central zones experience reduced speeds due to flow dissipation and recirculation. The upper and lower trays are more exposed to velocity variations, with localized zones of both high-speed jets and low-speed recirculation, which diminish overall uniformity. In contrast, moving farther from the center of the supply fans along the z-axis (Fig. 9 (b)) results in a more balanced distribution, with airflow across the 32 trays (16 on each side) becoming relatively uniform. This configuration produces a consistent velocity range of 0.82–1.9 m/s, providing favourable drying conditions and marking a significant improvement over recent studies 4 , 26 – 29 . Nevertheless, residual non-uniformities persist. Low-speed recirculation near the lower trays can lead to under-drying, while high-speed jet impingement near the upper trays may cause localized over-drying. These effects highlight the practical limitations of the current optimization: even with careful fan placement, achieving full uniformity is constrained by the inherent flow physics, including boundary layer effects, momentum dissipation, and geometric asymmetries within the cabinet 12 , 14 , 30 . To further mitigate these residual non-uniformities, future geometric modifications could be explored beyond fan positioning. Potential strategies including fine-tuning baffle angles and configurations to guide airflow more evenly, introducing flow straighteners or perforated panels to reduce jet impingement, and adjusting tray spacing or inlet/outlet shapes to minimize recirculation zones. Implementing such modifications has been shown to improve both airflow speed and temperature uniformity 7 , 15 , 16 , 31 , bringing multi-tray cabinet dryers closer to ideal drying conditions. Table 6 presents a comparative summary of recent related studies, highlighting similarities in the optimization of supply fan positions and other geometrical parameters for enhanced airflow distribution in multi-tray cabinet dryers.

This study presented an integrated Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) and Sequential Linear Programming (SLP) approach to optimize airflow distribution in a cabinet-type multi-tray dryer. Using orthogonal experimental design and polynomial regression modelling, the influence of supply fan positions on airflow uniformity was systematically evaluated. The regression model exhibited high predictive accuracy with a coefficient of determination (R² = 0.9247) and RMSE of 0.0037, validating the robustness of the model. The optimization processes achieved a notable enhancement in the airflow uniformity index (U i ), reaching a maximum value of 76.6% at optimal fan positions. This study achieved a uniform airflow range of 0.82–1.9 m/s, confirming the effectiveness of CFD-based optimization in enhancing drying uniformity. These findings underscore the significance of fans positioning in enhancing the airflow uniformity of multi-tray cabinet dryers. When compared to recent studies, a significant improvement in airflow uniformity has achieved. To improve the optimization’s convergence behavior, trust-region strategies were introduced. Compared to the SLP method without trust regions, which required approximately 661 iterations, the use of static and dynamic trust-region mechanisms significantly accelerated convergence, reducing the iteration count to 15 and 8, respectively without substantially altering the optimal result. Notably, the dynamic trust-region method demonstrated the fastest convergence rate with minimal zigzagging, offering more efficient navigation of the solution space. The trust-region approach dynamically controls the step size, eliminating the need for manually enforced small steps and contributing to improved stability and speed. This integrated CFD-SLP-trust region framework provides a scalable and computationally efficient tool for optimizing airflow in drying systems. Its versatility also opens potential for application in other thermal or fluid process optimization tasks across food, pharmaceutical, and chemical industries. Overall, these findings underscore the critical influence of supply fan positioning on airflow uniformity in multi-tray cabinet dryers. While the CFD-SLP approach provides valuable insights applicable to full-scale operations, the absence of experimental validation and thermal coupling remains a key limitation of this study. The optimum airflow uniformity represents a significant improvement in flow distribution. However, it does not necessarily ensure uniform drying, as temperature uniformity may become the next limiting factor. Therefore, future research should integrate thermal uniformity and perform comprehensive experimental validation under practical conditions to establish a complete and reliable optimization framework for multi-tray drying systems.
